course.title: Decision Theory
course.description: How to choose well when outcomes are uncertain: expected value, utility and risk, decision trees, the value of information, updating beliefs, and where real choosers depart from the theory.
course.audience: A capable adult comfortable with percentages and simple probability. They have met conditional probability and expected value and some basic game theory, and want a working method for real choices.

paragraphs: A company that launches a product has to commit before it knows whether the market will boom or slump, and a doctor reading a positive test result has to act before anyone can say for certain that the condition is there. Decision theory is the study of choices made in that position. It writes a choice out as the options you can pick, the states of the world you cannot control and the payoff of each pairing, and then asks which option is best given what you know or believe about how likely each state is.

Much of the subject is arithmetic you can check by hand. Weighting each payoff by its probability gives an uncertain option a single value that can be set against a sure amount, and the same reasoning puts a price on a forecast or a test before you decide whether to buy it. Where that arithmetic and ordinary judgement disagree, as they do over a coin game whose expected prize is unlimited but which almost nobody would pay much to play, the theory has had to be refined, and the refinements say a good deal about how people value money and risk.

The theory describes how a consistent chooser would decide, and real people do not always decide that way. Measuring where they depart from it, for instance by choosing differently when the same choice is described in terms of losses instead of gains, lets you tell a mistake you would want to correct from a preference the simple theory had left out.
outcomes: You'll be able to lay a choice out as options, states and payoffs, drop dominated options, and compare the rest by expected value.
You'll be able to roll back a decision tree to the best first move, and apply maximin and minimax regret when no probabilities are known.
You'll be able to compute a certainty equivalent and a risk premium, and say what a utility curve implies about risk.
You'll be able to update a probability with Bayes' rule and price information, perfect or imperfect, before buying it.
You'll be able to name the main ways real choices depart from expected utility, and find dominant strategies and equilibria in a two-by-two game.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Probability and Statistics, Economics: Markets and Strategy.

modules.title: Choosing with numbers
modules.description: Lay a choice out as options, states and payoffs, then use probability to compare options by expected value, in a table or a tree, and see what to do when no probabilities are known.

modules.title: Value and risk
modules.description: Money is a poor measure of value. Utility explains why a sure thing can beat a better average, and gives risk attitudes an exact meaning.

modules.title: Information and belief
modules.description: Update probabilities with Bayes' rule, then price the information itself: what it is worth to learn the state before choosing.

modules.title: Real choosers and other choosers
modules.description: Where people depart from expected utility, and what changes when the other side of the table is a player and not the weather.

concepts.title: State of the world
concepts.summary: A way things might turn out that you do not control and cannot choose, such as 'it rains' or 'demand is high'.

concepts.title: Payoff
concepts.summary: The value, in one stated unit, of choosing a given option when a given state turns out to hold.

concepts.title: Dominance
concepts.summary: Option X dominates option Y when X pays at least as much as Y in every state and strictly more in at least one.

concepts.title: Expected value
concepts.summary: The sum over outcomes of probability times payoff; the average payoff over many repetitions.

concepts.title: Net payoff
concepts.summary: The payoff after subtracting what the option costs to take.

concepts.title: Decision node
concepts.summary: A point in the tree where the chooser picks a branch.

concepts.title: Chance node
concepts.summary: A point where nature picks a branch with stated probabilities.

concepts.title: Rolling back
concepts.summary: Working from the leaves to the root, replacing each chance node by its expected value and each decision node by its best branch.

concepts.title: Maximin
concepts.summary: Choose the option whose worst payoff is largest.

concepts.title: Regret
concepts.summary: In a given state, the best payoff available in that state minus the payoff you got.

concepts.title: Minimax regret
concepts.summary: Choose the option whose largest regret across states is smallest.

concepts.title: St Petersburg game
concepts.summary: A coin is tossed until the first head; if that is on toss n the prize is 2^n. Its expected value is unbounded, yet few would pay much to play.

concepts.title: Utility
concepts.summary: A number on a scale such that the chooser prefers the gamble with the larger expected utility.

concepts.title: Diminishing marginal utility
concepts.summary: Each extra unit of money adds less utility than the one before, so the utility curve is concave.

concepts.title: Certainty equivalent
concepts.summary: The sure amount with the same utility as the gamble.

concepts.title: Risk premium
concepts.summary: The gamble's expected value minus its certainty equivalent.

concepts.title: Risk attitude
concepts.summary: Averse if utility is concave, neutral if linear, seeking if convex.

concepts.title: Prior
concepts.summary: The probability of a hypothesis before the new evidence.

concepts.title: Likelihood
concepts.summary: The probability of the evidence if the hypothesis is true.

concepts.title: Posterior
concepts.summary: The probability of the hypothesis after the evidence: P(H|E) = P(E|H) P(H) / P(E).

concepts.title: Expected value of perfect information
concepts.summary: Expected value of choosing after learning the state, minus expected value of the best choice now.

concepts.title: Value of the best choice now
concepts.summary: The highest expected value among the options before any information arrives.

concepts.title: Expected value of sample information
concepts.summary: Expected value of choosing after a real, imperfect test, minus expected value of the best choice now.

concepts.title: Pre-test and post-test
concepts.summary: Before the test you only have probabilities of each result; after it you use the posterior to choose.

concepts.title: Independence
concepts.summary: If you prefer gamble X to gamble Y, you still prefer a mixture of X and Z to the same mixture of Y and Z.

concepts.title: Transitivity
concepts.summary: If A is preferred to B and B to C then A is preferred to C.

concepts.title: Money pump
concepts.summary: Someone with cyclic preferences will pay a small fee for each trade round the cycle and end up where they began, poorer.

concepts.title: Loss aversion
concepts.summary: A loss weighs more heavily than an equal gain.

concepts.title: Framing
concepts.summary: Describing the same outcomes as gains or as losses changes the choice.

concepts.title: Sunk cost
concepts.summary: Money already spent and gone whatever you now choose; it should not affect a forward-looking choice.

concepts.title: Chooser vs player
concepts.summary: A state of the world does not react to your choice; another player does.

concepts.title: Dominant strategy
concepts.summary: A strategy that is best against everything the other player might do.

concepts.title: Nash equilibrium
concepts.summary: A pair of strategies where each is the best reply to the other.

lessons.title: Options, states and payoffs

lead.text: The launch decision has three kinds of ingredient. The launches A, B and C are the **options**: they are the things the company can choose between, and it picks exactly one. Boom, flat and slump are **states** of the world, ways things might turn out that the company does not control and cannot select, and exactly one of them will hold.

afterFigure.text: Every pairing of an option with a state has a result, written as a number in a single stated unit, here thousands of dollars, and called a **payoff**. Options down the side, states along the top and a payoff in every cell make a **payoff table**, and the whole decision fits inside it.
A common slip is to put a state among the rows. *The market booms* is not something the company can choose, so it heads a column however much the company might wish to choose it.

reveal.text: 'Open on Sunday' is something the owner picks, so it sits in a row, and the rain that may fall that day heads a column.

steps.headline: Build the payoff table for a café choosing between outdoor and indoor tables.

workedSteps.text: The options are the two things the owner picks between: tables outdoors or tables indoors. The states are sun and rain.
A payoff here is revenue minus cost. Going outdoors costs 40 dollars to set up in either state, and indoors costs nothing extra.
Indoors, the revenue is the payoff: 120 in sun and 130 in rain.
Outdoors in sun, the revenue is 180, so the setup cost leaves 140.
Outdoors in rain, the revenue is only 50, and the setup cost is the same as in sun.

reveal.text: B is never ahead of A in any state, and the next screen gives that pattern a name.

lead.text: A pays more in the boom, 50 against 40, the same in the flat market, 30 against 30, and more in the slump, 10 against 5, so there is no state in which B does better. When one option pays at least as much as another in every state, and strictly more in at least one, it **dominates** the other, and the other option is **dominated**.

afterFigure.text: The words *every state* carry the weight of the definition. Set A against C and the picture changes: C pays more in the boom, 80 against 50, but less in the flat market and in the slump, so A does not dominate C, and C, which loses in two states, does not dominate A either.
Dominance asks for a result that holds whichever state turns out, which is why it needs no probabilities at all.

diagram.alt: Two rows of the payoff table compared cell by cell. Against B, option A pays more in the boom and the slump and the same in the flat market. Against C, option A pays less in the boom and more in the other two states.
diagram.caption: Green marks the larger payoff, grey a tie and red the smaller. Use the buttons to compare A with B and then A with C.

reveal.text: N is never ahead of M and M is ahead in two states, so M dominates N and N could be removed from the table.

lead.text: Since A does at least as well as B whichever state arises, nobody who has read the table has a reason to choose B. Removing B therefore changes nothing about the choices worth weighing, and the table shrinks to A and C.

afterFigure.text: That is as far as dominance goes. A and C each win somewhere, C in the boom and A in the flat market and the slump, so neither can be removed, and the table still does not say which to launch.
To decide between them the company needs some idea of how likely each state is.

lessons.orientation: Lay a choice out as options, states and payoffs, and remove any dominated option.
lessons.nextAction: Attach probabilities to the states and compute the expected value of each option.

blocks.text: A company has finished developing a product and can launch it in one of three ways: A, a modest launch, B, a launch on cheaper terms, and C, an ambitious launch that spends heavily on stock and advertising. What each earns depends on something nobody at the company controls, which is whether the market turns out to be booming, flat or in a slump. In thousands of dollars, A earns 50 in a boom, 30 in a flat market and 10 in a slump, B earns 40, 30 and 5, and C earns 80, 20 and a loss of 20.
Those nine numbers are the whole decision, and no further fact about the product would change them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to lay a choice out as a payoff table and remove any option that another option matches or beats in every state.
intro.whyItMatters: A table makes a choice checkable, and dominance can settle part of it before anyone has to guess a probability.

recap.keyIdea: A choice becomes a table of options, states and payoffs, and an option that is never better than another and sometimes worse is dominated and can be dropped.

blocks.text: You laid the launch decision out with options as rows, states as columns and a payoff in every cell, and compared rows cell by cell. A dominates B because it pays at least as much in every state and more in two, whereas A and C each win somewhere and so stay in the table.
Dominance removes only the options that are never worth choosing, and what remains still has to be compared some other way.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson gives each state a probability, so that the options left in the table can be compared by one number each.

lessons.title: Expected value

reveal.text: The answer sits far above the midpoint of the two prizes, because the larger prize comes up so much more often. The next screen sets out the calculation.

lead.text: Take a gamble with three possible prizes: a 20% chance of winning 100, a 50% chance of winning 40, and a 30% chance of losing 10. A prize that comes up half the time should count for more in any summary of the gamble than one that comes up three times in ten, so each payoff is multiplied by its probability before the results are added. That gives 0.2 × 100 = 20, 0.5 × 40 = 20 and 0.3 × (−10) = −3, and their sum, 37, is the gamble's **expected value**.
Before multiplying anything it is worth checking that the probabilities add up to 1, because the outcomes are meant to cover everything that can happen. Here 0.2 + 0.5 + 0.3 = 1.

afterFigure.text: The 100 contributes no more than the 40, since it is two and a half times as large but only 0.4 times as likely, and the loss of 10 subtracts 3.

steps.headline: Find the expected value of a gamble that pays 80 with probability 0.25, 20 with probability 0.25 and −10 with probability 0.5.

workedSteps.text: First check that the probabilities cover every case.
Weight the first prize by its probability.
Weight the second prize in the same way.
The third prize is a loss of 10, and it comes up with probability 0.5.
Add the three products to get the expected value.

lead.text: Expected value is easily read as the result you should expect to see, and it is not that. In a single play of the gamble above you receive 100, 40 or −10, and 37 is none of them. What 37 describes is the average over many plays: the more times the gamble is played, the closer the running average of the prizes settles to the expected value, a result known as the law of large numbers.

afterFigure.text: After 10 plays the average is still pulled about by whichever prizes happened to come up, after 100 it has narrowed, and after 1000 it sits close to the dashed line at 37.

reveal.text: The expected value of one play multiplies up with the number of plays, which is why a long-run average is useful to anyone who plays often.

lead.text: A ticket costs $5 and pays $20 with probability 0.3 and nothing otherwise. Its expected prize is 0.3 × 20 + 0.7 × 0 = 6 dollars, but the buyer handed over 5 to get it, so the **net expected value** is 6 − 5 = 1 dollar. Quoting the 6 as the gain is a frequent mistake, because the 6 is what comes back and not what is left.

afterFigure.text: A sure amount is a gamble with one outcome of probability 1, so its expected value is simply the amount, and choosing by expected value means taking whichever option has the larger one.

reveal.text: The expected prize of 3 is smaller than the $4 price, so the ticket loses money on average although some tickets win a good deal.

lead.text: The wheel has 37 pockets, numbered 0 to 36, so the bet wins with probability 1/37 and loses with probability 36/37. Its expected net gain is therefore 35/37 − 36/37 = −1/37, which is about −0.027 per unit staked.

afterFigure.text: Over thousands of spins the average closes in on −0.027 per unit, and that gap, small for the player and steady for the house, is how a casino makes its income from a game in which it often pays out.

lessons.orientation: Compute the expected value of a gamble, subtract its price, and compare it with a sure amount.
lessons.nextAction: Draw a choice as a decision tree and work backwards from the end to find the best first move.

blocks.text: A single-number bet at European roulette stakes 1 and pays 35 if the ball lands on that number, and the wheel has 37 pockets. On any one spin the bettor ends up either 35 ahead or 1 behind. Yet the bet is usually summarised by a single number that is a fraction of a unit, and that number decides whether the game is worth playing at all.
The number is the bet's **expected value**, and it is worked out from the possible results and how often each occurs, before the wheel is spun.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute the expected value of a gamble, subtract the price of playing, and compare the result with a sure amount.
intro.whyItMatters: One number lets you compare a gamble with a sure thing before anything is played.

recap.keyIdea: The expected value of a gamble is each payoff times its probability, added up, and its net value is that figure less the price of playing.

blocks.text: You weighted each payoff by its probability, checked that the probabilities summed to 1, and added the results to get 37 for the three-prize gamble. That figure is an average over many plays rather than the outcome of one, and once the price is taken off it can be compared directly with a sure amount.
Applied to the launch table with probabilities of 0.3, 0.5 and 0.2, it ranked A above C even though C holds the largest single payoff.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson puts a sequence of choices and chances into a decision tree, and works back from the end to find the best first move.

lessons.title: Decision trees

lead.text: The square at the left is a **decision node**: it is where you choose, and each branch leaving it is one of your options. The circle on the stall's branch is a **chance node**: it is where the weather decides, each branch leaving it is one thing that might happen, and each carries a probability. Exactly one branch will occur, so the probabilities leaving a chance node must add to 1, here 0.6 + 0.4.

afterFigure.text: The end of every path is a **leaf**, and the number written there is the net payoff of arriving by that path. The entry fee of 200 is paid by anyone who takes the stall, whatever the weather, so it comes off both stall leaves (900 − 200 = 700 and 300 − 200 = 100), whereas the indoor market has no fee and stays at 400.

diagram.alt: A decision tree for a market day. A square decision node leads to two options: an outdoor stall, which reaches a circular chance node with sun at probability 0.6 and rain at 0.4, and an indoor market that pays 400. The second view shows net payoffs at the leaves, 700, 100 and 400.
diagram.caption: Squares mark choices, the circle marks chance, and each leaf holds a net payoff. Use the buttons to see takings first and then net payoffs.

reveal.text: The fee is paid whichever way the weather goes, so it comes off the rainy leaf too.

lead.text: To find the best first move, work from the leaves towards the root, which is called **rolling back** the tree. The chance node on the stall's branch is settled first, because its leaves are known, and its value is the expected value of those leaves: 0.6 × 700 + 0.4 × 100 = 420 + 40 = 460. That one number now stands for the whole stall branch, with the weather folded into it.

afterFigure.text: The decision node comes next, and it is simpler, because you choose and so it takes the *larger* of its branches in place of an average. The stall is worth 460 and the indoor market 400, so the stall is the better first move.

diagram.alt: The market-day tree rolled back in three stages. First the leaves 700, 100 and 400. Then the chance node is valued at 460. Then the decision node picks the stall, with 460 against 400 for the indoor market.
diagram.caption: Rolling back starts at the leaves. The chance node takes the weighted sum, and the decision node takes the larger branch.

steps.headline: Roll back a tree with two options: P reaches a chance node with a 0.3 chance of a net 200 and a 0.7 chance of a net 20, and Q is a sure 70.

workedSteps.text: The probabilities leaving P's chance node must add to 1.
Roll the chance node back by weighting each leaf by its probability. The 200 leaf contributes first.
The 20 leaf is weighted in the same way, and the node's value is the sum of the two weighted leaves.
Q is a leaf, so its value is the 70 written on it. The decision node takes the larger branch.
The first move is P, which is ahead of Q by 4.

reveal.text: The last chance node comes first, because nothing after it is still unknown. The next screen rolls the whole tree back.

diagram.alt: A two-stage decision tree. Option A leads to a chance node that pays 100 with probability 0.5 or reaches a second chance node, which pays 200 with probability 0.4 or 0 with probability 0.6. Option B pays 85 for certain.
diagram.caption: Option A has two chance nodes in a row. Option B is a single sure payoff.

lead.text: Option A pays 100 with probability 0.5, and otherwise reaches a second gamble that pays 200 with probability 0.4 and nothing with probability 0.6. The last chance node is valued first, because its leaves are known: 0.4 × 200 + 0.6 × 0 = 80. That 80 now stands in for the second gamble, and the first chance node can be treated as having two leaves, 100 and 80.

afterFigure.text: Its value is 0.5 × 100 + 0.5 × 80 = 50 + 40 = 90, and the decision node compares that with the sure 85 of option B and takes A, by 5.

A frequent slip is to put the second gamble's probabilities on the first branch as well, which weights them twice. Each probability belongs to the one branch it labels, and the nesting does the multiplying: the 200 is reached with probability 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2, but only because the 0.4 sits beyond the 0.5 and not beside it.

diagram.alt: The two-stage tree rolled back. The second chance node is worth 80, the first is worth 90, and the decision node compares 90 for option A with 85 for option B.
diagram.caption: Work from the last chance node back. Use the buttons to move through the three stages.

steps.headline: Roll back a two-stage tree and compare A with the sure option B.

workedSteps.text: A pays 60 with probability 0.5 and otherwise reaches a chance node that pays 100 with probability 0.2 and 20 with probability 0.8, while B is a sure 50.
Start at the chance node nearest the leaves, since its leaves are plain payoffs.
That node's value stands in for the whole second gamble in the rest of the tree.
Treat that value as a leaf, and roll back the first chance node.
The sure option B is worth 50, so the decision node takes B, by 2.

lead.text: A tree can hold a decision after a chance node as well as before it. Suppose that on a sunny day the stall owner can hire a helper for 150, which raises takings to 1300, and that on a rainy day the owner can close early, which cuts takings to 80 but leaves the entry fee to be paid. Each of these is its own decision node, and the leaves show net payoffs: 900 − 200 = 700 without a helper in the sun and 1300 − 200 − 150 = 950 with one, and 300 − 200 = 100 staying open in the rain against 80 − 200 = −120 closing early.

afterFigure.text: Rolling back starts, as always, at the leaves. In the sun the helper gives 950 against 700, so that decision node is worth 950, and in the rain staying open gives 100 against −120, so that node is worth 100. The chance node then weights those two values, 0.6 × 950 + 0.4 × 100 = 570 + 40 = 610, which beats the indoor market's 400.
The result is more than a first move. It is a **plan**: take the stall, hire the helper if it is sunny, and stay open if it rains, which says what to do in every circumstance that can arise.

diagram.alt: A decision tree with decisions after the chance node. Taking the stall leads to a chance node: sun at 0.6 leads to a choice between normal, worth 700, and hiring a helper, worth 950; rain at 0.4 leads to a choice between staying open, worth 100, and closing early, worth minus 120. The indoor market is worth 400. Rolled back, the stall is worth 610.
diagram.caption: Decisions can sit after chance nodes. Use the buttons to see the leaves and then the rolled-back plan.

lessons.orientation: Draw a decision tree with decision and chance nodes, and roll it back to the best first move.
lessons.nextAction: Choose when no probabilities are known, using rules such as maximin and minimax regret.

blocks.text: A weekend market offers two ways to earn a day's money. An outdoor stall costs 200 to enter and takes 900 if the day is sunny but only 300 if it rains, and the forecast gives a 60% chance of sun. A place in the indoor market has no extra cost and pays 400 whatever the weather does. The first option is two numbers joined by a forecast and the second is a single number, so they cannot be set side by side as they stand.

The choice also has an order to it, since you commit to the stall or to the indoor market first, and only afterwards does the weather decide. A **decision tree** draws the choice in that order, with each cost and probability placed where it arises.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to draw a choice as a decision tree, roll it back from the leaves, and read off the best first move and the plan that follows.
intro.whyItMatters: A tree puts each cost and probability where it arises, so a long choice can be worked one node at a time.

recap.keyIdea: A decision tree is rolled back from its leaves, with each chance node taking the probability-weighted sum and each decision node taking its largest branch.

blocks.text: You drew the market-day choice as a tree, with a square for the decision, a circle for the weather and a net payoff at each leaf, and rolled it back to 460 for the stall against 400 for the indoor market. Trees with two stages are rolled back from the last chance node, and a tree with later decisions gives a plan as well as a first move.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks what to do when the probabilities on a chance node are not known at all.

lessons.title: When no probabilities are known

lead.text: A pessimist looks at the worst that can happen under each option, which is 10 for A, −20 for C and 35 for D. Choosing the option whose lowest payoff is largest is the rule called **maximin**, and here it picks D, which guarantees at least 35 whatever the market does.

afterFigure.text: An optimist reverses the question and looks at each option's best payoff instead. Choosing the option whose highest payoff is largest is the rule called **maximax**. Neither rule uses more than one number from each row, which is why both are easy to apply and why both ignore so much: maximin takes no notice of how much D gives up in a boom, and maximax takes none of the loss that C risks.

reveal.text: Maximax chooses by the single highest payoff, so it accepts C's loss of 20 in a slump.
That shortfall has a name, and it is the basis of a third rule, which the next screen sets out.

lead.text: Suppose C is launched and the market turns out flat. C pays 20, but in a flat market D would have paid 40, so the company has fallen 20 short of what it could have had. That difference is the option's **regret** in that state: the best payoff available in the state, minus the payoff of the option chosen. Regret is always measured against the best option *in the same column*, and not against the best number anywhere in the table, because the best launch in a slump is a different launch from the best in a boom.

afterFigure.text: Doing this for every cell gives a regret table, in which an option that is best in a state has regret 0 there. Each option then has a largest regret, its worst disappointment, and the rule called **minimax regret** chooses the option whose largest regret is smallest. It asks which choice the company could regret least, whichever state turns out.

steps.headline: Build the slump column of the regret table.

workedSteps.text: Find the best payoff in the column. The three options pay 10, −20 and 35 in a slump, so the best is 35.
A's regret is the best minus A's payoff.
C pays −20 in the slump, and its regret is found the same way.
D pays the best payoff in this column, so its regret is 0.

steps.headline: Build the boom column of the regret table.

workedSteps.text: The three options pay 50, 80 and 40 in a boom, so the best is 80.
C pays the best payoff in this column, so its regret is 0.
D pays 40, so its regret is the best minus 40.
A pays 50, and its regret is found the same way.

reveal.text: Minimax regret picks the option that can never fall far behind the best choice, whatever the state.

lead.text: On the launch table maximin picks D, minimax regret picks A and maximax picks C. The disagreement does not mean that one calculation is wrong. A table with nothing missing can still give three different answers.

afterFigure.text: Maximin is often called the cautious rule, which tempts people into treating it as the correct one. Here it gives up 40 against C in a boom, and it would reject an option that wins heavily in nearly every state because of one poor state, however unlikely that state is. Caution is an attitude to risk and not a proof that the choice is right.

lead.text: Maximin behaves as though the worst state were certain to occur, and maximax as though the best were. A third rule, traditionally credited to Laplace as the principle of insufficient reason, treats the states as equally likely when nothing favours any one of them and then compares expected values. With a probability of a third on each state, D's payoffs average (40 + 40 + 35) ÷ 3, about 38.3, and C's average (80 + 20 − 20) ÷ 3, about 26.7. Equal weights are a view about the market too, namely that a boom is as likely as a slump.

afterFigure.text: Which rule to use therefore depends on what is known. If the company has some evidence about the market, even a rough lean, then probabilities are better used than ignored, and the expected-value methods of the earlier lessons apply.

reveal.text: Equal weights can rank options differently from either maximin or minimax regret, so the choice of rule is a real choice.
F's largest regret is above A's, so adding F does not change the minimax regret choice.
Safe describes the guarantee, and a guarantee can cost a great deal in the states where another option does better.

lessons.orientation: Apply maximin, maximax and minimax regret to a payoff table, and see why they can disagree.
lessons.nextAction: Ask why money may be the wrong scale, using the St Petersburg problem and the idea of utility.

blocks.text: Return to the launch table, with option B dropped because A dominates it and a cautious option D added. A pays 50, 30 and 10 in a boom, a flat market and a slump, C pays 80, 20 and −20, and D pays 40, 40 and 35. The analysts who forecast the market have looked at the evidence and decline to put a number on any state: nothing like the product has been sold before, and they say any figure for the chance of a boom would be invented.

The last lesson weighted every chance node by its probability, and here there is nothing to weight with. Several rules have been proposed for this case, each turning three rows of payoffs into one choice, and they need not agree.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to apply maximin, maximax and minimax regret to a payoff table, build its regret table, and say why the rules can pick different options.
intro.whyItMatters: When no probabilities exist, the choice of rule is part of the choice, and knowing the rules shows what each assumes.

recap.keyIdea: Maximin judges an option by its worst payoff, minimax regret by its largest regret against the best option in each state, and the two can pick different options.

blocks.text: You applied maximin and maximax to the launch table, built a regret table column by column by subtracting each payoff from the best in its state, and applied minimax regret to it. Maximin chose D, maximax chose C and minimax regret chose A, because each rule ignores most of the table and each carries an implied view of the states.
The choice among them depends on what is actually known about the market.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks whether money is the right scale for a payoff at all, starting from a coin-tossing game with an infinite expected value.

lessons.title: Utility and the St Petersburg problem

reveal.text: Each extra toss halves the chance, a fact the next screen sets against a prize that doubles.

lead.text: The game is called the **St Petersburg game**. A fair coin is tossed until it first lands heads, and if that happens on toss n the player wins 2^n dollars. The chance of the first head on toss n is (1/2)^n, since it needs n − 1 tails followed by a head, and so each outcome contributes (1/2)^n × 2^n = 1 to the expected prize.

afterFigure.text: There is no last toss, so the terms 1 + 1 + 1 + … never stop, and the expected prize is larger than any number you name. If the game is capped at N tosses, with nothing paid when no head has come, only N terms remain, and the expected prize becomes finite.

Few people would pay more than a few dollars to play, and that is the paradox: expected value recommends any price at all, and the recommendation is plainly wrong. The game takes its name from the journal of the St Petersburg academy, where Daniel Bernoulli published his answer in 1738.

diagram.alt: Two views of the St Petersburg game. The first lists the chance, the prize and their product for a first head on tosses 1 to 4, and every product is 1. The second shows the expected prize if the game stops after n tosses, rising by 1 for every extra toss, to 10 at 10 tosses.
diagram.caption: Every possible outcome adds 1, so the expected prize grows by 1 for each toss the game allows. Use the buttons to switch views.

reveal.text: A cap makes the expected prize a sensible number, which suggests the trouble comes from the unlimited prizes.

lead.text: Daniel Bernoulli's reply was that the amount of money is the wrong thing to average. An extra thousand dollars matters a great deal to someone with almost nothing and hardly at all to someone who already has a million, so what an amount is worth depends on what the person has. A number that scores each amount in this way is called its **utility**, and the rule is to choose the option with the larger *expected utility*, the probability-weighted average of the utilities rather than of the amounts. Utility here is not a measure of happiness: it is a number on a scale chosen so that the person prefers the gamble with the larger average.

afterFigure.text: The simplest curve to calculate with is the square root, u(x) = √x, which the figure shows. A 25-dollar step from 0 to 25 raises the utility by 5, from 0 to 5, whereas the same step from 75 to 100 raises it by only about 1.3, from 8.66 to 10. A curve that climbs ever more slowly in this way shows **diminishing marginal utility**: each extra dollar adds less than the one before.
Any curve of this shape serves for the argument.

steps.headline: Compare a gamble paying 16 or 64 with equal chances with a sure 36, using u(x) = √x.

workedSteps.text: Convert each prize to utility before averaging.
The larger prize, with utility 8, comes up with probability 0.5.
The utility of the smaller prize, weighted, is 0.5 × 4 = 2, so the expected utility is the sum.
A sure 36 has utility √36 = 6, the same as the gamble's expected utility, so the chooser is indifferent between them, though the gamble's expected prize is 0.5 × 16 + 0.5 × 64 = 40.

reveal.text: The expected prize is 50, but the expected utility is lower than the utility of 50, which the next screen uses.

steps.headline: A sure amount over a gamble

lead.text: The gamble of 0 or 100 has an expected utility of 5, while a sure 30 has utility √30, about 5.48, which is higher, so a chooser with this curve takes the sure 30 even though the gamble's expected prize is 50. The figure shows why: the dashed chord joining the two prizes lies below the curve, and the gamble sits at its midpoint, while the sure amount sits on the curve itself.

afterFigure.text: This is not an error in the person's reasoning. The curve records how much each amount is worth to them, and a flattening curve says that the second 50 dollars is worth less than the first, so a gamble that risks the first for a chance at the second is worth less than its prize average suggests.
The rule stays the same for everyone, which is to choose the option with the highest expected utility, and the utility function carries the person's attitude to risk.

lead.text: Score each prize with u(x) = log₂ x, so that the prize 2^n has utility n. The outcome with the first head on toss n then contributes (1/2)^n × n, and the terms are 1/2, 2/4, 3/8, 4/16, and so on, which shrink quickly enough for the total to settle at 2. A sure amount with utility 2 is 2^2 = 4 dollars, so a chooser with this curve values the whole unbounded game at 4 dollars, close to what people actually say they would pay.

afterFigure.text: The version here scores the prize alone, whereas Bernoulli added each prize to the player's existing wealth, but the lesson is the same. The paradox shows that the thing averaged, an amount of money, was the wrong thing to average, and that a utility which grows more slowly than the prize gives the game a finite worth.

reveal.text: Reading a utility back as an amount is how a gamble gets a single sure price, which the next lesson develops.
The curve is part of the description of the person's preferences, so a flattening curve is a fact about the chooser, not a mistake in the arithmetic.

lessons.orientation: See why expected money can mislead, and compute expected utility with a concave utility function.
lessons.reviewLabel: Utility and the St Petersburg problem
lessons.nextAction: Turn expected utility back into a sure amount, and use it to describe attitudes to risk.

blocks.text: A fair coin is tossed until it lands heads, and if the first head comes on toss n you win 2^n dollars: 2 if it comes at once, 4 if it takes two tosses, 8 if it takes three, and so on without end. Work out the expected prize in the way the earlier lessons did, and you find that it is larger than any number you could name.

Yet almost nobody would hand over more than a few dollars to play, so either the people are wrong or expected prize is the wrong measure. Daniel Bernoulli's answer, published in 1738, was to score each prize by what it is worth to the player instead of by its size in dollars, an idea now called **utility**.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say why expected money can mislead, and to compute the expected utility of a gamble with a flattening utility curve.
intro.whyItMatters: It shows when a gamble with the larger expected prize is still the worse choice, and why.

recap.keyIdea: Utility values an amount by what it is worth to the chooser, and choosing the highest expected utility replaces choosing the highest expected prize.

blocks.text: The St Petersburg game has an unbounded expected prize, since every outcome adds 1, and yet it is worth little to most people. Bernoulli's reply was to average utility, with each extra dollar adding less than the one before, and with u(x) = √x a sure 30 beats a gamble of 0 or 100 even though that gamble's expected prize is 50.
A flattening curve is therefore no flaw in the chooser. It is the thing that carries the chooser's attitude to risk.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns expected utility back into a sure amount, the certainty equivalent, and reads a person's attitude to risk from the shape of the curve.

lessons.title: Risk attitudes and certainty equivalents

reveal.text: That sure amount has a name, and the next screen reads it from the curve.

lead.text: The figure shows the gamble of 16 or 64 on the square-root curve. Its expected utility is 6, halfway between the utilities 4 and 8, and the sure amount with that utility is found by reading across to the curve and down to the axis, which gives 36. That amount is called the **certainty equivalent** of the gamble: the sure sum that the chooser values exactly as much as the gamble itself.

afterFigure.text: The gamble's expected value is 40, higher than the certainty equivalent of 36, and the gap between them is the **risk premium**. Here it is 4, and it is the most the chooser would give up of the gamble's expected prize to have a sure amount in its place.

diagram.alt: A graph of the square-root utility curve for amounts from 0 to 80 dollars, with the gamble of 16 or 64 shown as a dashed chord. The expected utility, 6, sits at the middle of the chord. Reading across to the curve and down gives the sure amount 36, and the gap between 36 and the expected value 40 is the risk premium, 4.
diagram.caption: Read the expected utility across to the curve, then down to the amount. Use the buttons to follow the steps.

steps.headline: Find the certainty equivalent, the expected value and the risk premium of a gamble paying 4 or 36 with equal chances, for u(x) = √x.

workedSteps.text: Convert each prize to utility.
The expected utility is the average of the two utilities.
The sure amount with that utility is the gamble's certainty equivalent.
The expected value of the prizes is 0.5 × 4 + 0.5 × 36 = 20, so the risk premium is the expected value minus the certainty equivalent.

reveal.text: A wider spread of prizes gives a larger premium, which is why risk matters more as the stakes grow.

lead.text: The figure puts one gamble, 0 or 10 with equal chances, on three curves. On the **concave** curve, which flattens as the amount grows, the certainty equivalent is 2.5, well below the expected value of 5, and the chooser is **risk averse**. On the straight line the certainty equivalent equals the expected value, and the chooser is **risk neutral**. On the **convex** curve, which steepens, the certainty equivalent is 7.07, above the expected value, and the chooser is **risk seeking**, so that the gamble is valued above its average prize.

afterFigure.text: Notice which way round this runs, since it is easy to reverse: a concave curve means *averse*. The scale of the curve does not matter, because multiplying every utility by a positive number leaves every comparison unchanged, and it is the bend alone that carries the attitude. A risk-averse chooser therefore has a positive risk premium for every gamble, a risk-neutral one has a premium of zero, and a risk-seeking one has a negative premium.

diagram.alt: Three utility curves over amounts from 0 to 10, each with the gamble of 0 or 10 drawn as a dashed chord whose middle is the expected value, 5. For the concave curve the certainty equivalent is 2.5, below 5. For the straight line it is 5. For the convex curve it is 7.07, above 5.
diagram.caption: The same gamble on three curves. Use the buttons to see how the certainty equivalent compares with the expected value of 5.

reveal.text: The certainty equivalent lands above the expected value of 10, which is how a risk-seeking chooser's valuation looks.

lead.text: Take an owner with wealth 100 and u(w) = √w who faces a 10% chance of losing 50. Without insurance the owner's wealth is 100 with probability 0.9 and 50 with probability 0.1, so the expected utility is 0.9 × 10 + 0.1 × √50, about 9.71, and the expected wealth is 95. The sure wealth with utility 9.71 is 9.71² ≈ 94.23, and that is the certainty equivalent of the risk.

afterFigure.text: Paying a premium P leaves the owner with 100 − P for certain, so the owner is willing to pay until 100 − P falls to 94.23, which is a premium of about 5.77. The expected loss is only 0.1 × 50 = 5, so an insurer who charges anywhere between 5 and 5.77 covers its expected payout while leaving the owner better off than without cover.

diagram.alt: The square-root utility curve for wealth between 50 and 100. The uninsured owner has wealth 100 with probability 0.9 and 50 with probability 0.1, so expected utility 9.71 and expected wealth 95. The sure wealth with the same utility is 94.23, so the owner would pay up to 5.77 for insurance.
diagram.caption: The owner's expected wealth is 95, but the risk is worth only 94.23 to them. Use the buttons to read it off.

steps.headline: Find the most a homeowner with wealth 100 and u(w) = √w would pay for full cover against a 50% chance of losing 36.

workedSteps.text: Without cover the owner has wealth 100 or 64, each with probability 0.5.
The utilities are √100 = 10 and √64 = 8, so the expected utility is the average.
The sure wealth with utility 9 is 9² = 81.
Full cover leaves the owner with wealth 100 minus the premium, whichever way the risk would have turned out.

lead.text: Risk aversion is sometimes taken to mean refusing every gamble, and the curve says nothing of the kind. A chooser with wealth 100 and u(w) = √w who is offered a fair coin that wins 20 or loses 10 compares the expected utility of the bet with the utility of staying put, and the bet can come out ahead because its expected gain is large beside the premium that its risk costs.

afterFigure.text: The same chooser, with the same curve, turns down a coin that wins 50 or loses 40, although its expected gain is the same 5. Wealth would become 150 or 60, and the expected utility, 0.5 × √150 + 0.5 × √60, is about 9.997, just under the 10 that staying put gives. Behaviour therefore depends on the stakes as well as on the curve, and a chooser can be close to risk neutral for small amounts and clearly averse for amounts that threaten a large part of their wealth, because a curve is nearly straight over a short stretch.

reveal.text: The bet raises expected utility, so a risk-averse chooser accepts it. Averse describes the curve's bend and not a refusal to gamble.
The convex curve puts every certainty equivalent above the expected value, the reverse of the concave case.

lessons.orientation: Compute a certainty equivalent and a risk premium, and read a risk attitude from the shape of a utility curve.
lessons.nextAction: Update a probability with new evidence using Bayes' rule.

blocks.text: The last lesson met a chooser whose utility for money is the square root, valuing a gamble that pays 16 or 64 with equal chances. Its expected prize is 40 and its expected utility is 6, and that utility belongs to some sure amount of money, which can be read straight back off the curve.

The gap between that sure amount and the expected prize can be measured in dollars, and its size and sign depend on how the curve bends, so a single number describes a person's whole attitude to a gamble.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute a certainty equivalent and a risk premium, and to say from the shape of a utility curve whether a chooser is risk averse, neutral or seeking.
intro.whyItMatters: A sure amount lets you price a gamble, and the price shows how much a chooser dislikes or likes the risk.

recap.keyIdea: The certainty equivalent is the sure amount with the same utility as a gamble, the risk premium is the expected value minus it, and a concave curve means risk aversion.

blocks.text: You found the certainty equivalent by averaging utilities and undoing the utility function, 36 for the gamble of 16 or 64 against an expected value of 40, and read the premium of 4 from the gap. A concave curve gave a positive premium, a straight line gave zero and a convex curve gave a negative one.
Insurance followed from the premium: an owner averse to risk will pay more than the expected loss to be rid of it.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to evidence, and shows how a probability is revised when a test result arrives.

lessons.title: Updating beliefs with Bayes' rule

reveal.text: The chance is only about 9%, far below the 90% that it is tempting to read off the test, and the next screen finds it by counting people in groups.

lead.text: Suppose a condition affects 1% of those tested, and the test is positive for 90% of people who have it, a rate called its **sensitivity**, and also for 9% of people who do not, its **false-positive rate**. Take 10,000 people. Then 100 have it and 9,900 do not, and the test is positive for 90 of the 100 and for 891 of the 9,900.

afterFigure.text: The positives therefore number 90 + 891 = 981, and only 90 of them have the condition, so the chance that a person with a positive result has it is 90 ÷ 981, about 9.2%. The test is 90% sensitive, yet most of its positive results come from healthy people, because there are so many more of them.

diagram.alt: A frequency tree for 10,000 people tested for a condition with prevalence 1 percent. 100 have it and 9,900 do not. Of the 100, 90 test positive and 10 negative. Of the 9,900, 891 test positive and 9,009 negative. The positives total 981, of whom 90 have the condition.

reveal.text: Both groups contribute positives, which is why the total is larger than the true positives alone.

steps.headline: For the second test, find the chance that a person with a positive result has the condition.

workedSteps.text: Of 1,000 people, 50 have the condition and 950 do not.
The test is positive for 80% of the 50 and for 10% of the 950.
In total 135 people test positive, and 40 of them have the condition.
A positive result moves the chance from 5% before the test to about 29.6%, a large rise that still leaves the condition less likely than not.

lead.text: The counts have names. The probability before the evidence, here 0.01, is the **prior**. The probability of the observed result under each possibility, 0.9 with the disease and 0.09 without it, is the **likelihood**. The probability after the evidence is the **posterior**, and **Bayes' rule** gives it as P(H | E) = P(E | H) × P(H) ÷ P(E). In the example the numerator is 0.9 × 0.01 = 0.009, and P(E), the chance of a positive result for anyone, is 0.009 + 0.09 × 0.99 = 0.0981.

afterFigure.text: The ratio 0.009 ÷ 0.0981 is about 0.0917, the same 9.2% found by counting. The counting version is the one to reach for first, because every step of it is a number of people.

diagram.alt: Three boxes joined by arrows: prior, likelihood and posterior. The prior is the chance of disease before the test, 0.01. The likelihoods are the chance of a positive result with the disease, 0.9, and without it, 0.09. The posterior is the chance of disease after a positive result, about 0.092.
diagram.caption: Bayes' rule joins the three parts. Use the buttons to read each one.

lead.text: Mixing up the two conditional probabilities is the most common error, and it comes from ignoring the **base rate**, the prior chance in the population. Keep the test as it is, at 90% sensitivity and a 9% false-positive rate, and raise the prevalence from 1% to 10%. Of 10,000 people, 1,000 have it and 900 test positive, while 9,000 do not and 810 test positive, so a positive result now means a chance of 900 ÷ 1,710, about 52.6%.

afterFigure.text: A positive result from the very same test is a weak signal when the condition is rare and a strong one when it is common, and a test that is described as 90% accurate cannot be interpreted until the base rate is known. That is why the numbers to ask for are the prior, the sensitivity and the false-positive rate, and not a single accuracy figure.

diagram.alt: A curve of the chance of disease after a positive result against prevalence, for a test that is 90 percent sensitive with a 9 percent false-positive rate. At prevalence 1 percent the chance is 9.2 percent, at 10 percent it is 52.6 percent, and it rises steadily towards 100 percent.
diagram.caption: The same test gives very different answers for different base rates. The chance after a positive result depends on how common the condition is.

reveal.text: The word is common in spam and rare elsewhere, so the posterior is high though spam is the minority of mail.

lead.text: Updating again is easiest with odds. After one positive result the odds of disease against no disease are 90 : 891, which is the same as 10 : 99. The likelihood ratio, the chance of a positive with the disease over the chance without it, is 0.9 ÷ 0.09 = 10, and a second independent positive multiplies the odds by it once more: 90 × 10 : 891 = 900 : 891. The probability is then 900 ÷ 1,791, about 50.3%.

afterFigure.text: Each independent result multiplies the odds by its own likelihood ratio, and two results with a ratio of 10 give a factor of 100 on the odds, which is why the chance climbs from 1% to 9.2% to 50.3%. A frequent mistake is to add the likelihoods of two tests, or to add their ratios, and it fails because evidence combines by multiplication on the odds. The rule holds only when the two results are independent given the true state, which a repeated run of the very same flawed test may not be.

diagram.alt: Bars for the chance of disease: 1 percent before any test, 9.2 percent after one positive result, and 50.3 percent after two independent positive results.
diagram.caption: Each independent positive result multiplies the odds by the same factor, 10, so the chance climbs quickly once it is not tiny.

reveal.text: The odds route and the counting route always agree, and the odds route is the faster one when evidence arrives in several steps.
Evidence from independent sources multiplies, so even weak individual results can add up to strong evidence.

lessons.orientation: Revise a probability after a test result with natural frequencies and Bayes' rule, including a second independent result.
lessons.nextAction: Price perfect information by comparing the best choice now with the best choice after the state is known.

blocks.text: A screening test for a condition that affects 1% of the people tested picks up the condition in 90% of those who have it, and it also returns a positive result for 9% of people who do not. A patient is tested and the result is positive. It is tempting to take the 90% as the chance that the patient has the condition, since the test seems to be right nine times in ten.

The 90% describes how the test treats people who have the condition, while the patient needs the reverse, the chance that the condition is there given a positive result. The two can be very far apart, and **Bayes' rule** is the way to get from one to the other, using how common the condition was to begin with.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to revise a probability after a test result using counts of people and Bayes' rule, and to update again when a second independent result arrives.
intro.whyItMatters: Decisions that depend on evidence need the probability after the evidence, and that is rarely the number the test reports.

recap.keyIdea: A posterior is the prior revised by the likelihood of the evidence, and it can be found by counting people or by multiplying odds by a likelihood ratio.

blocks.text: You counted 10,000 people to find that a positive result from a 90% sensitive test, for a 1% condition and a 9% false-positive rate, means a chance of about 9.2%, and wrote the same calculation as Bayes' rule. The answer depends on the base rate, and a second independent positive result multiplies the odds by the likelihood ratio again, taking the chance to about 50.3%.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks what it is worth to learn the state of the world for certain before choosing.

lessons.title: What perfect information is worth

reveal.text: Knowing the failure lets you avoid the loss, and the next screen adds up that benefit over both states.

lead.text: Choosing now, the tree gives investing an expected value of 0.4 × 100 − 0.6 × 30 = 22, which beats 0, so the best choice now is worth 22. Suppose instead that a seer could tell the company, before it decides, whether the project will succeed. The company would invest only on success and stay out on failure, and the expected value would be 0.4 × 100 + 0.6 × 0 = 40.

afterFigure.text: The difference, 40 − 22 = 18, is the **expected value of perfect information**, usually shortened to EVPI: the expected value of choosing after learning the state, minus the expected value of the best choice now. It is also the expected regret of investing now, 0.6 × 30 = 18, because the loss of 30 is exactly what the seer lets the company avoid in the 60% of cases where the project fails.

diagram.alt: Two decision trees for an investment that succeeds with probability 0.4 and pays 100, or fails with probability 0.6 and loses 30, against not investing, which pays 0. Choosing before learning the state gives expected value 22. Learning the state first gives 40, because you invest only on success. The difference is 18.
diagram.caption: Two orders of events for the same project. Use the buttons to compare them and read the difference.

reveal.text: That number is the baseline against which any forecast has to be measured.

steps.headline: Find the EVPI of the second project.

workedSteps.text: The best choice now is investing, worth 0.5 × 60 − 0.5 × 20 = 20.
With a perfect forecast the company invests only on success, so the value is 0.5 × 60 + 0.5 × 0.
The forecast raises the company's expected value from the first figure to the second.
Check against the expected regret of investing: the loss of 20 happens half the time.

lead.text: No real forecast can do better than a perfect one, so the EVPI is the ceiling on the price of any information about the state. For the first project it is 18. At 12 the company ends with 40 − 12 = 28, above the 22 it has by choosing now, so buying pays. At 25 it would end with 40 − 25 = 15, below 22, so the forecast costs more than it can ever bring in.

afterFigure.text: Information is worth the decisions it changes and nothing else. If investing were the best choice in every state, no forecast could alter the decision and the EVPI would be 0. And since the EVPI describes a perfect forecast, it must not be mistaken for the price of a real, imperfect one, which is always worth less.

diagram.alt: A number line from 0 to 45 with the value of the best choice now, 22, and the value with a perfect forecast, 40, marked and joined by a bracket labelled expected value of perfect information, 18. A forecast priced at 12 leaves 28, above 22. One priced at 25 leaves 15, below 22.

reveal.text: The forecast clears the bar by 4, which is the EVPI of 18 less its price of 14.
Information that cannot change the decision cannot improve it, so it is worth nothing.
The nearer the company is to being sure, the less a forecast can correct, so the ceiling on its price falls.
The EVPI bounds the value of an imperfect forecast from above, and working out its actual value is the next lesson's task.

lessons.orientation: Compute the expected value of perfect information and use it as a ceiling on what to pay for any information.
lessons.nextAction: Price a real, imperfect test by combining Bayes' rule with a decision tree.

blocks.text: A company can invest in a project that succeeds with probability 0.4 and pays 100, or fails with probability 0.6 and loses 30, and not investing pays nothing. Investing has an expected value of 22 and so is the better choice as things stand, yet it loses 30 in six cases out of ten. A consultant says that for a fee she can tell the company, before it decides, whether the project will succeed.
Knowing the answer would change what the company does in the failure cases, and that change has a value in money, called the **expected value of perfect information**.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute the expected value of perfect information for a choice, and use it to reject any price for information that exceeds it.
intro.whyItMatters: It gives a ceiling for the price of any information before any test is designed or bought.

recap.keyIdea: The expected value of perfect information is the value of choosing after learning the state minus the value of the best choice now, and it caps what any information is worth.

blocks.text: You compared the best choice now, worth 22, with the choice made after learning the state, worth 40, and the difference of 18 is the expected value of perfect information. It equals the expected regret of the best choice now, it falls to 0 when no forecast could change the decision, and it caps the price of any real, imperfect source of information.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson prices a real test, which is imperfect, by combining Bayes' rule with a decision tree.

lessons.title: Paying for a test

reveal.text: That probability is the weight of the test's good branch, and the next screen builds the whole tree around it.

lead.text: A test is run before the decision, so the tree starts with a chance node for the result. Before the test, all that is known is how likely each result is: here P(good) = 0.4 × 0.8 + 0.6 × 0.3 = 0.5, and P(bad) is the other 0.5. After a result is seen, the choice is made with the posterior probability of success, found with Bayes' rule. After good it is 0.4 × 0.8 ÷ 0.5 = 0.64, and after bad it is found in the same way, from the 0.2 chance that the test says bad when the project will succeed.

afterFigure.text: On the good branch investing has a 0.64 chance of paying 100 and a 0.36 chance of losing 30, and the bad branch carries its own posterior, which you can work out next. Because the decision follows the result, each branch has its own decision node, and the two nodes can choose differently.

diagram.alt: A two-stage decision tree. A test comes first and says good with probability 0.5 or bad with probability 0.5, and each result leads to a choice to invest or not. After good, the chance of success is 0.64 and of failure 0.36. After bad, the chances are left blank. Investing pays 100 on success and −30 on failure, and not investing pays 0.
diagram.caption: Test first, then decide. The posteriors after a bad result are left for you to find.

steps.headline: Choose the best action after each result of the test.

workedSteps.text: After a good result the chance of success is 0.64 and of failure 0.36.
Investing pays 100 on success and loses 30 on failure.
After a bad result the chances are 0.16 and 0.84, so investing is worth 0.16 × 100 − 0.84 × 30.
Not investing pays 0, which beats −9.2, so the plan is to invest after a good result and to stay out after a bad one.

lead.text: Weighting the two branches by the probability of each result gives the value of acting on the test: 0.5 × 53.2 + 0.5 × 0 = 26.6. The best choice now was worth 22, so the **expected value of sample information**, written EVSI, is 26.6 − 22 = 4.6. The test is worth 4.6 on average, and that is the most it should cost.

afterFigure.text: The cost of the test belongs to the whole test and not to one branch, since it is paid whatever the result. Take it off the value with the test, and compare with 22: a test costing 3 leaves 23.6, which beats 22, whereas a test costing 5 leaves 21.6, which does not. Perfect information gave a ceiling, and the EVSI gives the actual price limit for this test.

diagram.alt: The test-then-decide tree rolled back: investing is worth 53.2 after good and minus 9.2 after bad, so you invest only after good, and the test node is worth 26.6. Then bar charts: the best choice now is 22, the test 26.6 before its cost, a perfect forecast 40. A test costing 3 leaves 23.6, above 22, and one costing 5 leaves 21.6, below it.

lead.text: Consider a weaker test that says good with probability 0.6 if the project will succeed and 0.5 if it will fail. After a bad result the chance of success is 0.16 ÷ 0.46, about 0.35, and investing is still worth about 15.2, so the company would invest after either result. The decision never changes, so the test, though it carries some evidence, has an EVSI of 0 and is worth nothing at any price.

afterFigure.text: Two habits cause trouble here. One is to read the test's accuracy as the probability of success, whereas the probability after a good result also depends on the prior, as the 0.64 and 0.16 did. The other is to subtract the test's cost from the payoffs of one branch only, which breaks the comparison. Each branch of a test is reached only by paying for the test, so the cost belongs to the total.

reveal.text: The test never changes the choice, so it never adds value, however carefully it has been designed.
The same test and the same good result give a different posterior, so the test's accuracy cannot be read as the chance of success.
The price is compared with the test's own EVSI, and the EVPI only guarantees that no test can be worth more than 18.

lessons.orientation: Use Bayes' rule inside a decision tree to find the expected value of sample information and decide whether a test is worth its cost.
lessons.nextAction: Check choices against the axioms of expected utility, starting with the Allais paradox.

blocks.text: The last lesson priced a perfect forecast at 18 for a project that succeeds with probability 0.4, paying 100, or fails with probability 0.6, losing 30. No forecast is perfect, and the one on offer is a test that says good 80% of the time when the project will succeed and 30% of the time when it will fail. Its result will raise or lower the chance of success without settling it.

A test that is sometimes wrong is worth less than a perfect one, and putting Bayes' rule inside a decision tree tells you how much less, as a single amount of money that can be set against the test's fee.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to build a test-then-decide tree, compute the expected value of sample information, and decide whether a test is worth its cost.
intro.whyItMatters: It prices real tests and forecasts, which are always imperfect, before you pay for them.

recap.keyIdea: The expected value of sample information is the value of choosing after a real test minus the value of the best choice now, found by updating with Bayes' rule on each result.

blocks.text: You put a test in front of the decision, found each result's probability and the posterior after it, chose the best action after each, and weighted by the results to reach 26.6 against 22 for choosing now. The difference of 4.6 is the most the test can be worth, well below the 18 of perfect information, and a test that never changes the choice is worth nothing.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson steps back from calculation and asks whether the expected-utility rule itself holds up, beginning with the Allais paradox.

lessons.title: The axioms and the Allais paradox

lead.text: John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern showed in 1944 that if a person's preferences over gambles satisfy a few axioms, then there is a utility function whose expected value the person is maximising. In plain words the axioms are four. The preferences must be **complete**, so any two gambles can be compared, and **transitive**, so that preferring A to B and B to C means preferring A to C. They must be **continuous**, so that no gamble is infinitely better than another, and they must satisfy **independence**: if you prefer gamble X to gamble Y, you still prefer a mixture of X with a third gamble Z to the same mixture of Y with Z.

afterFigure.text: Independence is the most demanding of the four, because it says that a part of the outcome that is shared by both options should play no part in the choice between them. Transitivity is the simplest to test, and a chooser who breaks it can be exploited.

reveal.text: A cycle of preferences cannot be ranked, and it can also be turned into a loss, which the next screen shows.

lead.text: Suppose you hold C and prefer B to C, A to B and C to A. A trader offers to swap C for B for a fee of 1, which you accept because you prefer B. The trader then offers A for B for another fee of 1, and then C for A for a third fee of 1, and each swap is one you are glad to make. After three swaps you hold C again, having paid 3, and the trader can repeat the cycle for as long as you will accept it. The loss is called a **money pump**.

afterFigure.text: Nothing in any single step looks like a mistake, which is why an argument from the money pump is persuasive: cyclic preferences are not only unusual but expensive.

diagram.alt: Three items A, B and C joined by arrows in a cycle. A person who prefers B to C, A to B and C to A pays 1 to swap C for B, 1 to swap B for A and 1 to swap A for C, and is back holding C after paying 3.
diagram.caption: The cycle of preferences: each swap is one the person is glad to pay for. Use the buttons to take the swaps in turn.

reveal.text: The cost grows with every trip, which is why the cycle is described as a pump.
That value is the small number against which the next screen sets the other three gambles.

lead.text: In a standard modern form, with amounts in millions of dollars, the first choice is between A, which pays 1 million for certain, and B, which pays 1 million with probability 0.89, 5 million with probability 0.10 and nothing with probability 0.01. The second choice is between C, which pays 1 million with probability 0.11 and nothing otherwise, and D, which pays 5 million with probability 0.10 and nothing otherwise.

afterFigure.text: B has the higher expected value, 0.89 × 1 + 0.10 × 5 = 1.39 million against 1, yet many people take the certainty of A, since B carries a 1% chance of ending with nothing. In the second pair neither gamble is certain, the chances of winning, 11% and 10%, are close, and the prize in D is five times larger, so many people take D.

lead.text: Take u for the utility function. Preferring A to B means u(1M) > 0.89 u(1M) + 0.10 u(5M) + 0.01 u(0), and subtracting 0.89 u(1M) from both sides leaves 0.11 u(1M) > 0.10 u(5M) + 0.01 u(0). Preferring D to C means 0.10 u(5M) + 0.90 u(0) > 0.11 u(1M) + 0.89 u(0), and subtracting 0.89 u(0) from both sides leaves 0.10 u(5M) + 0.01 u(0) > 0.11 u(1M). The two inequalities say the same two quantities are in opposite orders, so no values of u(0), u(1M) and u(5M) satisfy both.

This answers a natural objection, that the chooser merely has a utility curve for money that bends, since the contradiction does not depend on the shape of the curve. The paradox is about how probabilities are used, and the shared 89% in the figure on the previous screen is what produces it: it is 1 million in the first pair and nothing in the second, and expected utility says it should cancel, whatever it is.

steps.headline: Test the two preferences with a particular utility scale, u(nothing) = 0 and u(1M) = 1, and see what each requires of u(5M).

workedSteps.text: Preferring A to B requires 0.11 u(1M) > 0.10 u(5M) + 0.01 u(0), which with this scale reads 0.11 > 0.10 u(5M).
That inequality limits how large u(5M) can be.
Preferring D to C requires 0.10 u(5M) > 0.11, which means u(5M) is above that same limit.
No number is both below and above 1.1, so the two preferences cannot both come from this scale, and a different scale gives the same contradiction.

reveal.text: Independence says the shared part should not matter, and the pattern shows that for many people it does.

lead.text: It would be a mistake to conclude that the people who choose A and D are foolish. Independence is an assumption of the theory, and the Allais pattern is a measured failure of the assumption. One response is to hold the axiom as a standard of rational choice and to treat the pattern as an error to be corrected. The other is to keep the description of what people do and weaken the axiom.

afterFigure.text: Both responses agree on what has been shown: expected utility with a single utility function makes a definite prediction, and the prediction fails for a common pair of choices.

reveal.text: The two pairs differ only in the shared 89%, which cancels from both inequalities, so no curve can make A over B and D over C agree.

lessons.orientation: State what an expected-utility maximiser must satisfy, and show that a common pair of choices cannot be explained by any utility function.
lessons.reviewLabel: The axioms and the Allais paradox
lessons.nextAction: Describe how real choosers value gains and losses, using prospect theory, framing and sunk cost.

blocks.text: Here are two choices, and the question is which you would take in each. In the first you can have 1 million dollars for certain, or a gamble with an 89% chance of 1 million, a 10% chance of 5 million and a 1% chance of nothing. In the second you can have an 11% chance of 1 million, or a 10% chance of 5 million.

A great many people take the sure million in the first and the 5 million in the second, and each choice looks sensible when it is made. Maurice Allais showed in 1953 that no way of valuing money, however curved, makes both choices follow from maximising expected utility.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to state the requirements of expected utility, spot a money pump, and show why the Allais choices cannot come from any utility function.
intro.whyItMatters: It shows exactly what the expected-utility rule demands, and where real choices part from it.

recap.keyIdea: Expected utility needs transitive and independent preferences, and the common Allais pattern of choices breaks independence for every possible utility function.

blocks.text: You met the axioms behind expected utility and saw that a cycle of preferences breaks transitivity and can be turned into a money pump. The Allais choices, A over B and D over C, require u(5M) to be both below and above 1.1 on one scale, so the failure lies in independence and not in the curvature of the utility function.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson describes how real choosers value gains and losses, and how framing and sunk costs pull choices away from the theory.

lessons.title: Prospect theory, framing and sunk cost

reveal.text: The two programmes have the same expected result, and the next screen shows what happens when people are asked to choose.

lead.text: Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman put this problem to two groups of people in a study published in *Science* in 1981.

afterFigure.text: A and C describe the same outcome, since saving 200 of 600 leaves 400 dead, and B and D describe the same gamble. Yet in the first wording 72% of the respondents chose the sure option A, while in the second 78% chose the gamble D. The choice reversed with the wording, although every number is the same. Describing identical outcomes as gains or as losses is called **framing**.

diagram.alt: Bars for two wordings of a choice about 600 people at risk. A saves 200 for sure; B saves 600 with probability one third and nobody otherwise. C means 400 die; D means nobody dies with probability one third and 600 die otherwise. The third view shows that A and C are the same outcome, and so are B and D.

reveal.text: Applied to programme D, the same weighting gives (2/3) × 600 = 400 expected deaths, equal to the 400 certain deaths of programme C, so the two wordings describe the same choice.

lead.text: Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 paper, 'Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk', explains such reversals by changing what is valued. People judge an outcome as a gain or a loss from a **reference point**, usually the status quo, and not by the final amount they hold. The value function drawn from that point has two features: it flattens as gains or losses grow, and it is steeper for losses than for gains, so that a loss weighs more than an equal gain. This is called **loss aversion**.

afterFigure.text: The simple model on the second view uses straight lines, with slope 1 for gains and slope 2 for losses, so that a loss counts twice as much as a gain of the same size. The framing problem then follows from the reference point: in the first wording the outcomes are gains relative to 600 deaths, where people avoid risk, and in the second they are losses relative to everyone surviving, where people accept a risk to avoid a sure loss.

diagram.alt: Two value functions drawn around a reference point at the centre. The schematic curve rises steeply and then flattens for gains, and falls more steeply and then flattens for losses, steeper than the gains side. The simple model is two straight lines, with slope 1 for gains and slope 2 for losses, and a gamble of plus 100 or minus 60 has value minus 10.
diagram.caption: Value is measured from a reference point and is steeper for losses than for gains. Use the buttons to see the schematic curve and the simple model.

steps.headline: Value a 50/50 gamble that wins 100 or loses 60, in a model where losses count twice.

workedSteps.text: The expected money value is 0.5 × 100 − 0.5 × 60 = 20, so a chooser who ignores loss aversion would accept.
In the model the gain is worth its size, so the gain term is 0.5 × 100.
The loss is the other half of the gamble, and in this model it counts twice.
The value is the sum of the two terms, which is below zero, so the chooser declines a bet with a positive expected money value.

reveal.text: The win has to be larger than twice the loss, which is why a loss-averse chooser turns down many bets with a positive expected money value.

lead.text: Suppose you paid 80 for a ticket to an event, and the money is not refundable. On the day you would sooner not go: travelling costs 30, and the event is worth 20 to you. Going costs 80 for the ticket, 30 for travel and gains 20 of enjoyment, a total of −90, while skipping costs only the 80, a total of −80. The 80 is a **sunk cost**: it has been spent and is gone whichever way you choose.

afterFigure.text: Because the sunk cost sits in both columns, it cannot make going better than skipping, and removing it leaves the comparison of −10 against 0, which tells you to skip. Many people go because they paid, which is the **sunk-cost fallacy**. Past spending is not irrelevant in every way: it matters when it tells you something about the future, such as a ticket you could resell. The mistake is to let money that cannot change what happens next decide what you do next.

diagram.alt: A table comparing going to an event with skipping it. The 80 already paid for the ticket appears in both columns. Going adds 30 of travel and 20 of enjoyment, so its total is minus 90 against minus 80 for skipping. Leaving out the 80, which is the same in both, going is minus 10 and skipping is 0.
diagram.caption: The 80 sits in both columns, so it cannot make one option better than the other. Use the buttons to compare the two views.
