reveal.text: The ticket price does not help to compare the two options, because you lose it either way.
The outcomes did not change, so the shift is a property of how the choice was framed, and consistent choosers would not show it.

lessons.orientation: Use a reference-dependent value function to explain loss aversion and framing, and recognise sunk-cost reasoning.
lessons.reviewLabel: Prospect theory, framing and sunk cost
lessons.nextAction: Treat choices where another player responds, and find best replies and dominant strategies.

blocks.text: Six hundred people are at risk from a disease, and you must choose between two programmes. Programme A saves 200 people for certain, and programme B saves all 600 with probability one third and nobody with probability two thirds. A different group is offered programmes C and D, which are described by deaths: C means that 400 people die, and D means that nobody dies with probability one third and 600 die with probability two thirds.

The programmes in the second description are the same as in the first, with the same outcomes and the same chances, so a consistent chooser would pick the same programme in both. Real choosers often do not, and the way their choices shift with the wording, along with the weight they give to losses and to money already spent, is what **prospect theory** and the study of framing set out to describe.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to value a gamble with a reference point and loss aversion, recognise a framing effect, and spot a sunk cost.
intro.whyItMatters: It explains why real choices drift from expected utility in systematic ways, and how to catch them in yourself.

recap.keyIdea: People value outcomes as gains or losses from a reference point, weigh losses more than gains, and so can reverse a choice when the same outcomes are reframed.

blocks.text: You saw the same disease choice in two wordings, 72% choosing the sure option as lives saved and 78% choosing the gamble as deaths in the 1981 study, and explained the reversal with a reference point and a steeper value for losses. With losses counting twice, a gamble of +100 or −60 has value −10 and is declined, and a sunk cost, which appears in every option, should play no part in a forward-looking choice.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson asks what changes when the state of the world is another player who responds to what you choose.

lessons.title: When the state fights back

reveal.text: That is the method of the earlier lessons, and the next screen asks whether it is the right method when the other side has aims of its own.

lead.text: Another person can be treated in the same way when you hold a belief about what they will do. Suppose the other player will play Left with probability 0.7 and Right with probability 0.3, and that you choose between Up, which pays 4 against Left and 1 against Right, and Down, which pays 2 against Left and 3 against Right.

afterFigure.text: Down's expected payoff is 0.7 × 2 + 0.3 × 3 = 2.3, and Up's is 3.1, so against this belief Up is the better reply. The method is the one you already have, and its quality depends entirely on the belief, which was supplied from outside.

diagram.alt: A two-by-two payoff table for you, with options Up and Down against the other player's moves Left and Right. Up pays 4 against Left and 1 against Right. Down pays 2 against Left and 3 against Right. The other player is believed to play Left with probability 0.7. The second view adds expected values, 3.1 for Up and 2.3 for Down.
diagram.caption: Treat the other player's move as a state with a probability. Use the buttons to add the expected values.

lead.text: A state of the world does not react to your choice, but another player does. They also want something, and they know that you do, so what they will do depends on what they expect of you, and a fixed probability for their move leaves that out. The figure shows the best-known case, the **prisoner's dilemma**, in which each player chooses to cooperate or to defect and each cell shows your payoff first and the other's second.

afterFigure.text: Two ideas make it possible to reason about the other player without a guessed probability. Your **best reply** to a move of theirs is the choice that pays you most against that move. A **dominant strategy** is one that is a best reply to every move the other player might make, so that you do not need to know what they will do.

diagram.alt: A two-by-two table for the prisoner's dilemma. If both cooperate, each gets 3. If you cooperate and the other defects, you get 0 and they get 5. If you defect and the other cooperates, you get 5 and they get 0. If both defect, each gets 1.
diagram.caption: Each cell shows your payoff first and the other player's second.

reveal.text: A dominant strategy needs no belief about the other player, since it is best whatever they do.

steps.headline: Check each cell of the prisoner's dilemma to see whether either player would want to switch.

workedSteps.text: At (cooperate, cooperate) you get 3. If you alone switch to defect you get 5, so you would switch, and this cell is not stable.
At (defect, defect) you get 1, and you could switch to cooperate while the other player still defects.
The other player is in the same position, because the table is symmetric: switching alone would leave them with less.
Neither player gains by switching alone, so (defect, defect) is a **Nash equilibrium**: a pair of strategies in which each is the best reply to the other.

lead.text: John Nash defined the equilibrium in a one-page paper of 1950, and it is the answer to the question of where a belief could come from: in an equilibrium each player's strategy is the best reply to the other's, so the belief each holds about the other is correct. Defecting is your best reply to cooperation and to defection, and it is the other player's best reply too, so both play it and the result is (defect, defect), with 1 each.

afterFigure.text: It is tempting to read an equilibrium as the best outcome for both, and here it is not, because (cooperate, cooperate) would give each player 3. Neither player can reach it alone, since a player who cooperates against a defector gets 0, and so the dilemma is that each player's best reply leads both to a worse result.

diagram.alt: The prisoner's dilemma table with best replies marked. Your best reply is to defect whatever the other does, and the other's best reply is also to defect. The cell where both defect, payoffs 1 and 1, is the equilibrium, though both would get 3 if both cooperated.
diagram.caption: Mark each side's best replies, then see where they meet. Use the buttons to move through the three views.

(3, 3) would suit both better.</text></svg>

reveal.text: Each player's best reply is the same whatever the other does, so both end at (Down, Right) with 1 each, although (Up, Left) would give each of them 2.
A dominant strategy for the other player tells you what to expect from them, and your own best reply follows.
Once the other player's choice is settled by dominance, your own best reply completes the equilibrium.

lessons.orientation: Say what changes when the other side chooses, and find dominant strategies and equilibria in a two-by-two game.
lessons.nextAction: You can now set out a choice as options, states and payoffs, value it with expected utility, price information, and check the result against how choosers behave.

blocks.text: The weather has no interest in whether you carry an umbrella, so in the earlier lessons a state of the world could be given a probability and left alone. A competitor deciding on a price is different, because the competitor has payoffs too, knows that you do, and chooses with your choice in mind.

A belief about that competitor's move can still be turned into a probability, and then the choice is an ordinary expected-value problem, but it is not obvious where such a belief could come from when the competitor is reasoning about you in the same way.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say how a player differs from a state of the world, find a dominant strategy in a two-by-two game, and find its equilibrium.
intro.whyItMatters: Many real choices are made against someone who is also choosing, and the method for a state of the world does not apply unchanged.

recap.keyIdea: A state of the world does not react to your choice but another player does, and a dominant strategy or an equilibrium of best replies replaces a guessed probability.

blocks.text: You compared treating the other player as a state, with a probability on each move, to reasoning about their payoffs. In the prisoner's dilemma defecting is a dominant strategy for each player, so (defect, defect) is the equilibrium, although both would be better off at (cooperate, cooperate).
The same tools apply to any two-by-two game: look for a dominant strategy for each player, and then check that each strategy is a best reply to the other.

questions.prompt: A café owner is deciding whether to open on Sunday, and the day's takings depend on whether it rains. In the owner's payoff table, which of these heads a column?
hints: Ask who decides each one: the owner, or the world?
What the owner picks sits in the rows.
questions.onCorrect: The owner cannot choose the rain, so it heads a column. Opening and staying closed are the owner's choices, so each sits in a row.

misconceptions.feedback: Staying closed is the owner's other choice, so it is also a row. Ask which of the three the owner cannot pick.
Opening is something the owner picks, so it is one of the rows. Ask who decides each of the three.

questions.prompt: A café can put its tables outdoors, at a setup cost of 40 dollars, or keep them indoors at no extra cost. Revenue is 180 dollars outdoors in sun and 50 dollars outdoors in rain; indoors it is 120 in sun and 130 in rain. Payoff is revenue minus cost. What is the payoff of going outdoors when it rains?
hints: The payoff is revenue minus whatever the option costs.
Outdoors costs 40 to set up, whichever state holds.
Take the rainy-day outdoor revenue, 50, and subtract the cost.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The revenue is 50 and the setup cost is 40, so the payoff is 50 − 40 = 10.

questions.onCorrect: The setup cost comes off every outdoor payoff: 180 − 40 = 140 in sun, and 50 − 40 = 10 in rain.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the revenue. The setup cost of 40 is paid in either state, so it comes off.

questions.prompt: In how many of the three states does option B pay strictly more than option A? (A pays 50, 30, 10 and B pays 40, 30, 5.)
hints: Compare the payoffs in one column at a time.
In the flat market both options pay 30.
Count only the columns where B's number is larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: B pays less than A in the boom (40 < 50) and the slump (5 < 10), and the same in the flat market (30 = 30), so in none.

questions.onCorrect: In the flat market B only ties A. B is never ahead, which is what a dominated option looks like.

misconceptions.feedback: In the flat market B pays 30 and so does A. A tie is not strictly more.
B pays less than A in two states and ties in the third.

questions.prompt: In how many states does option C (80, 20, −20) pay more than option A (50, 30, 10)?
hints: Compare the two rows one column at a time.
C is ahead in the boom. What about the other two columns?
Count the columns where C's number is the larger one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: C pays more only in the boom (80 > 50). In the flat market 20 < 30 and in the slump −20 < 10.

questions.onCorrect: C wins in the boom alone, so A does not dominate C, and C does not dominate A.

misconceptions.feedback: C is ahead only in the first column. In the other two its payoff is smaller.
C's payoffs in the flat market and the slump are lower than A's.

questions.prompt: Option X pays 5, 5, 5, option Y pays 6, 5, 4 and option Z pays 4, 5, 6 across three states. How many of the three options are dominated?
hints: Dominance needs one option to be at least as good in every state.
Compare X with Y: is Y at least as good as X in the third state?
Check each of the three pairs for a row that never falls behind.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Y beats X in the first state and loses in the third, Z does the reverse, and Y and Z trade places too. No option is at least as good as another everywhere, so none is dominated.

questions.onCorrect: Each pair splits the states, one ahead in the first and the other ahead in the third, so no row is beaten everywhere.

misconceptions.feedback: Y beats X in the first state, but in the third it pays 4 against X's 5. One win does not give dominance.
Every pair has a state where each option is ahead, so neither dominates the other.

questions.prompt: Option Q pays 70, 25 and 5 in three states, and option P pays 70, 20 and 5. Q ties P in two states and beats it in one. What term from this lesson describes P in relation to Q?
hints: Q is never behind P and is ahead once.
One word names the option that is beaten this way.
questions.onCorrect: Q dominates P: it pays at least as much in every state and strictly more in one, so P is the dominated option.

misconceptions.feedback: That word names Q, which pays at least as much as P everywhere. P is on the other side of that relation.

questions.prompt: Payoffs in thousands of dollars in Boom, Flat and Slump: A pays 50, 30, 10; B pays 40, 30, 5; C pays 80, 20, −20. Which option is dominated by another?
hints: Look for a row that is never ahead of another row.
Compare A with B in each of the three states.
questions.onCorrect: A pays more than B in the boom and the slump and the same in the flat market, so B is dominated by A.

misconceptions.feedback: A is ahead of B and, in the boom, behind C. It is not beaten in every state by any option.
C is beaten by A in two states but pays more in the boom, so it is not dominated.
Compare each pair of rows, state by state, before deciding that nothing is dominated.

questions.prompt: In how many states does A (50, 30, 10) pay strictly more than B (40, 30, 5)?
hints: Compare the two rows column by column.
Mark each column as more, equal or less.
Count the columns marked more.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A pays more in the boom (50 > 40) and in the slump (10 > 5), and ties in the flat market (30 = 30).

questions.onCorrect: The tie in the flat market is why dominance asks only for 'at least as much' everywhere and 'more' somewhere.

misconceptions.feedback: In the flat market both pay 30, which is a tie rather than strictly more.
A is also ahead in the slump, 10 against 5.

questions.prompt: Option Z pays 60, 25, 10 in Boom, Flat, Slump. Does Z dominate A, which pays 50, 30, 10?
hints: Dominance has to hold in every state.
Compare the two rows in the flat market.

acceptedIdeas: No: it pays less in Flat
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No: it pays less in Flat

questions.onCorrect: Z is ahead in the boom, level in the slump and behind in the flat market, 25 against 30, and one weaker state blocks dominance.

choices.label: No: it pays less in Flat

misconceptions.feedback: Z wins the boom, but dominance has to hold in every state. Check the other two states as well.
A tie is allowed. Look at the other states for what blocks dominance.
Dominance is checked state by state and needs no probabilities.

questions.prompt: A gamble pays 90 with probability 0.9 and nothing with probability 0.1. What is its average prize per play in the long run?
hints: The two prizes do not come up equally often.
Weight each prize by its probability before adding.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 90 comes up nine times in ten, so the average is 0.9 × 90 + 0.1 × 0 = 81.

questions.onCorrect: The average is pulled towards the prize that comes up nine times in ten, so it is far above the midpoint of 45.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain average of 90 and 0, which treats the two prizes as equally likely. They are not.
That ignores the 10% of plays that pay nothing.

questions.prompt: The third prize of the gamble is −10, and it comes up with probability 0.5. What is that prize weighted by its probability?
hints: Half of 10 is 5.
The prize is a loss, so the product is negative.
Keep the minus sign when you multiply.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Half of −10 is −5.

questions.onCorrect: The loss counts against the total: 0.25 × 80 + 0.25 × 20 − 5 = 20, which is the gamble's expected value.

misconceptions.feedback: The prize is a loss, so the product keeps its minus sign.

questions.prompt: The gamble with a 20% chance of 100, a 50% chance of 40 and a 30% chance of −10 has an expected value of 37 per play. What total is expected over 1,000 plays?
hints: The expected value is a long-run average per play.
Multiply the average per play by the number of plays.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each play contributes 37 on average, so 1,000 plays contribute 1,000 × 37 = 37,000.

questions.onCorrect: Over many plays the expected value adds up play by play, which is how a casino can predict its takings across a night.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the expected value of one play. The question asks for 1,000 plays.
100 is only the largest prize, and it comes up one play in five.

questions.prompt: A ticket costs $4 and pays $30 with probability 0.1, and nothing otherwise. What is the net expected gain per ticket, in dollars?
hints: First find the expected prize on its own.
0.1 × 30 is what the ticket returns on average.
Subtract the price of 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The expected prize is 0.1 × 30 = 3, and the price is 4, so the net is 3 − 4 = −1.

questions.onCorrect: A net of −1 means that buyers lose $1 per ticket on average, even though one ticket in ten returns far more than it cost.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the expected prize. The $4 price comes off it.
The $30 is won only one time in ten, so it is weighted by 0.1 first.

questions.prompt: Some wheels have 39 pockets: 18 red, 18 black and three green (0, 00 and 000). A bet of 1 on red pays 1 when red comes up and loses the stake otherwise. What is the expected net gain per unit staked, to three decimal places?
hints: Count the winning pockets and the losing ones out of 39.
Red wins with probability 18/39, and the other 21 pockets lose.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The bet wins 1 with probability 18/39 and loses 1 with probability 21/39, so the expected gain is 18/39 − 21/39 = −3/39 ≈ −0.077.

questions.onCorrect: On a single-zero wheel the same bet loses 1/37, about 0.027, per unit, so the two extra green pockets nearly triple the house's edge.

misconceptions.feedback: The bet is close to even, but all three green pockets lose a bet on red, so the expectation is below zero.
Each loss is 1 against a win of 1, so the loss comes from the 21 losing pockets against 18 winning, not from half the pockets.
That is the edge on a wheel with one green pocket. This wheel has three, so 21 of its 39 pockets lose a bet on red.

questions.prompt: The launch table from the previous lesson gives A payoffs 50, 30, 10, B payoffs 40, 30, 5 and C payoffs 80, 20, −20 in a boom, a flat market and a slump. Suppose the probabilities are 0.3, 0.5 and 0.2. What is the expected value of C, in thousands of dollars?
hints: Weight each of C's payoffs by the probability of its state.
The three products are 24, 10 and −4.
Add them, keeping the minus sign.
questions.onCorrect: The same weights give A 32 and B 28, so A has the best expected value although C has the largest single payoff.

misconceptions.feedback: That is C's best payoff, which occurs only 30% of the time.
That is the plain average of C's payoffs. Each state has its own probability.

questions.prompt: A gamble pays 100 or nothing with equal chances. You may instead take 45 for certain. By how much does the gamble's expected value exceed the sure amount?
hints: A sure amount is its own expected value.
Find the gamble's expected value first.
Subtract 45.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The gamble has expected value 0.5 × 100 + 0.5 × 0 = 50, and 50 − 45 = 5.

questions.onCorrect: By expected value the gamble wins by 5, though someone afraid of ending with nothing may still prefer the 45.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gamble's expected value. The question asks how far it is above 45.
That subtracts 45 from the top prize of 100, which the gamble pays only half the time.

questions.prompt: A gamble pays 200 with probability 0.1, 30 with probability 0.6 and −20 with probability 0.3. What is its expected value?
hints: First check that the probabilities add to 1.
Multiply each payoff by its own probability.
Add 20, 18 and −6.
questions.onCorrect: The 200 contributes most of the total even though it is the rarest outcome, because it is so much larger than the others.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain average of the three payoffs. The probabilities differ, so each payoff is weighted.
That adds the payoffs without weighting them.

questions.prompt: A ticket costs $8 and pays $50 with probability 0.1, and nothing otherwise. What is the net expected gain per ticket, in dollars?
hints: Find the expected prize first.
Subtract the $8 price.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The expected prize is 0.1 × 50 = 5 dollars, so the net is 5 − 8 = −3.

questions.onCorrect: A net of −3 means that the ticket costs 3 dollars more than it returns, on average.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the expected prize before the price comes off.
The prize is won with probability 0.1 only, and the price must be paid first.

questions.prompt: An American roulette wheel has 38 pockets. A single-number bet of 1 pays 35 when it wins and loses the stake otherwise. What is the expected net gain per unit staked, to three decimal places?
hints: The probabilities are 1/38 and 37/38.
Net gain is 35 on a win and −1 on a loss.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The bet wins 35 with probability 1/38 and loses 1 with probability 37/38: 35/38 − 37/38 = −2/38 ≈ −0.053.

questions.onCorrect: The extra pocket doubles the loss compared with a 37-pocket wheel, from about −0.027 to −0.053.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the 37-pocket wheel. This wheel has 38 pockets, so the probabilities change.
That is 35/38, the winning term alone. The losing term must be subtracted.

questions.prompt: A stall costs 150 to enter and takes 500 if the day is sunny. What number belongs at the sunny leaf, once every cost on the path has been taken off?
hints: The fee is paid on the stall's path, before the weather is known.
Subtract the entry fee from the takings.
500 minus 150.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The takings are 500 and the entry fee on that path is 150, so the leaf is 500 − 150 = 350.

questions.onCorrect: The fee is paid whichever way the weather goes, so it comes off the rainy leaf as well.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the takings. The entry fee belongs on the path that incurs it, so it comes off.
The fee is a cost, so it is subtracted from the takings.

questions.prompt: P's chance node has a 0.3 chance of a net 200 and a 0.7 chance of a net 20. What is the value of the node?
hints: Weight each leaf by its own probability.
The two products are 60 and 14.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: The node's value is its expected value, which now stands for the whole of P's branch.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain average of 200 and 20, which gives the two leaves equal weight.
That adds the leaves without weighting them.

questions.prompt: In the two-stage tree, option A leads to a chance node, one branch of which leads to a second chance node, and option B is a sure 85. Which value can be found first?
hints: Which node's leaves are all numbers already?
A node can be valued only when everything after it has a value.

acceptedIdeas: The second chance node, nearest the leaves
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The second chance node, nearest the leaves

questions.onCorrect: The second chance node has only ordinary payoffs after it, so it can be valued at once, and every node before it waits on it.

choices.label: They can be found in any order
The decision node at the root
The first chance node, nearest the root
The second chance node, nearest the leaves

misconceptions.feedback: The first chance node has a branch that leads to another node, so check whether everything after it is already known.
The root compares the values of its branches, so it comes last.
Some nodes cannot be valued until others have been, so the order is not free.

questions.prompt: The second chance node pays 100 with probability 0.2 and 20 with probability 0.8. What is its value?
hints: Weight each payoff by its probability.
The products are 20 and 16.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: That 36 now stands for the whole second gamble when the first chance node is rolled back.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain average of 100 and 20.
That adds the payoffs without weighting them.

questions.prompt: In the market tree, hiring a helper now costs 300, so the sunny leaf with a helper is 800. The other leaves are unchanged: 700 in sun without a helper, 100 in rain with the stall open, −120 in rain closing early. Sun has probability 0.6 and rain 0.4. What is the value of the stall branch?
hints: Roll back each decision node first, taking the larger leaf.
The sunny node is worth 800 and the rainy node is worth 100.
Weight those two values by 0.6 and 0.4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: In the sun the better choice is the helper, worth 800, and in the rain it is staying open, worth 100, so the branch is worth 0.6 × 800 + 0.4 × 100 = 480 + 40 = 520.

questions.onCorrect: The helper is still worth hiring in the sun, since 800 beats 700, but the stall's value has fallen from 610.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value with the helper at 150. The sunny leaf is now 800.
That ignores the helper option. The sunny decision node takes the larger leaf, 800.
That puts the early-closing leaf of −120 in the rain. A decision node takes the larger of its branches.

questions.prompt: A stall costs 250 to enter and takes 800 if the day is sunny, probability 0.5, or 200 if it rains, probability 0.5. What is the value of the chance node?
hints: Take the entry fee off both takings first.
The net leaves are 550 and −50.
Weight each leaf by 0.5 and add.
questions.onCorrect: The fee comes off both leaves, so the node's value is the expected takings, 500, less the fee, 250.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the expected takings. The entry fee has to come off the leaves first.
That is only the sunny leaf. The chance node weights both leaves.

questions.prompt: A stall costs 250 to enter and takes 800 in sun, probability 0.5, or 200 in rain, probability 0.5. The indoor market pays a sure 280. Which first move does the rolled-back tree choose?
hints: Roll back the chance node of the stall first.
The stall's net leaves are 550 and −50.
Compare the node's value with 280.
questions.onCorrect: The stall branch is worth 250, below the sure 280, so the decision node takes the indoor market.

misconceptions.feedback: The stall's best leaf is large, but a chance node is valued by weighting both of its leaves, not by taking the best one.
Roll the stall's chance node back and compare its value with 280. The two values are not the same.
The probabilities are given, 0.5 and 0.5, so the chance node can be valued.

questions.prompt: Option A pays 120 with probability 0.4, and otherwise reaches a second gamble that pays 300 with probability 0.3 and 0 with probability 0.7. What is A's value?
hints: Value the second gamble first.
It is worth 90, and it is reached with probability 0.6.
Weight 120 by 0.4 and 90 by 0.6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second gamble is worth 0.3 × 300 + 0.7 × 0 = 90, so A is worth 0.4 × 120 + 0.6 × 90 = 48 + 54 = 102.

questions.onCorrect: The second gamble is reached only 60% of the time, so its value of 90 is weighted by 0.6 and not by its own 0.3.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves the second gamble's value out of the 0.6 weight. It is reached only when the first branch fails.
That averages 120 and 90 as if the branches were equally likely, but they have probabilities 0.4 and 0.6.

questions.prompt: In a boom, a flat market and a slump, option A pays 50, 30 and 10, option C pays 80, 20 and −20, and option D pays 40, 40 and 35. Which option does maximax choose?
hints: Maximax looks at each option's best payoff only.
Find the best payoff of each option and compare them.
questions.onCorrect: Maximax ranks options by their best payoff alone, so it takes C's 80 and sets its loss of 20 aside.

misconceptions.feedback: A's best payoff is 50, and another option has a higher best payoff.
D has the best worst case, which is maximin's test. Maximax compares the best payoffs.

questions.prompt: The company launches A and the market falls into a slump, where A pays 10. In a slump the best option, D, would have paid 35. How much less did A pay than the best available option in that state?
hints: Compare A with the best payoff in the same state.
The best payoff in a slump is 35.
Subtract A's 10 from it.
questions.onCorrect: That difference of 25 is A's regret in a slump. It is measured against the best option in that state, whatever the other states hold.

misconceptions.feedback: That compares A with C's loss. Regret is measured against the best payoff in the state, which is 35.
That compares A with the best payoff anywhere in the table, 80. Regret uses the best payoff in the same state.

questions.prompt: In the slump column the best payoff is 35. What is C's regret there, where C pays −20?
hints: Subtract C's payoff from the column best.
C's payoff is negative.
35 minus −20 adds the two.
questions.onCorrect: Subtracting a negative payoff adds to the regret, which is why a loss in a state where another option does well hurts so much.

misconceptions.feedback: Subtracting −20 adds 20 to 35. Check the sign.
That is the column best. Regret is the gap between it and C's payoff.

questions.prompt: In the boom column the best payoff is 80. What is D's regret there, where D pays 40?
hints: Subtract D's payoff from the column best.
The column best is 80.
The column best, 80, is the first number in the subtraction.
questions.onCorrect: D's regret of 40 in a boom is the price of its caution, and it is D's largest regret.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the column best. Regret is its gap from D's payoff.
D does not match the best payoff in a boom, so its regret is not 0.

questions.prompt: In the regret table, option A has regrets of 30, 10 and 25, option C has 0, 20 and 55, and option D has 40, 0 and 0. Which option does minimax regret choose?
hints: Find the largest regret of each option.
Choose the option whose largest regret is the smallest.
questions.onCorrect: A's largest regret, 30, is the smallest of the three, so no outcome leaves the company further behind than 30.

misconceptions.feedback: C has regret 0 in a boom but 55 in a slump, the largest regret of the three.
D's largest regret is 40, which is larger than A's largest regret.

questions.prompt: A new option E pays 70, 30 and 0 in a boom, a flat market and a slump. If each state has probability 1/3, what is E's expected payoff, to two decimal places?
hints: Equal weights mean every state counts a third.
Add the payoffs.
Divide by 3.
questions.onCorrect: Equal weights amount to the claim that the three states are equally likely, which is itself a view about the market.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the payoffs without weighting them.
That leaves out the boom payoff before dividing by 3. All three states count, each with weight 1/3.

questions.prompt: Add option E, which pays 70, 30 and 0, to the table. The column bests are still 80, 40 and 35. What is E's largest regret?
hints: Work out E's regret in each of the three states.
The regrets are 10, 10 and something in the slump.
The largest is the slump regret.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: E's regrets are 80 − 70 = 10, 40 − 30 = 10 and 35 − 0 = 35, so the largest is 35.

questions.onCorrect: E's largest regret, 35, is above A's 30, so minimax regret would still choose A.

misconceptions.feedback: That is E's regret in the boom and the flat market. The slump regret is larger.
E is not the best option in any state, so none of its regrets is 0.

questions.prompt: A manager argues that maximin is the safe rule, so on the launch table it cannot lead the company wrong. Which reply is accurate?
hints: Maximin looks at one number from each option.
Think about what D gives up in a boom.

acceptedIdeas: Maximin guarantees the best worst case, but it can give up large gains.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Maximin guarantees the best worst case, but it can give up large gains.

questions.onCorrect: D guarantees at least 35 but gives up 40 against C in a boom, so maximin expresses caution and does not prove its choice best.

choices.label: Maximin picks the same option as minimax regret here, so the choice is settled.
Maximin needs the probability of each state, and none are known.
Maximin is valid only when every state is equally likely.
Maximin guarantees the best worst case, but it can give up large gains.

misconceptions.feedback: On this table maximin picks D and minimax regret picks A, so the rules differ.
Maximin uses only each option's worst payoff and no probabilities.
Maximin makes no assumption about how likely the states are.

questions.prompt: In three states, option P pays 60, 20 and 0, option Q pays 30, 30 and 25, and option R pays 100, 10 and −30. Which option does maximin choose?
hints: Find the lowest payoff of each option.
Maximin chooses the option whose lowest payoff is the largest.
questions.onCorrect: Q's worst case of 25 is the best of the three worst cases, so Q is the option that guarantees the most.

misconceptions.feedback: P's worst payoff is 0, which is below the worst payoff of one of the others.
R pays the most in the first state, but its worst payoff, −30, is the lowest of the three.

questions.prompt: For options P, Q and R above, the best payoffs by state are 100, 30 and 25. What is Q's largest regret across the three states?
hints: Subtract Q's payoff in each state from the best payoff in that state.
Q's regret in the first state is the biggest.
100 minus 30.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Q's regrets are 100 − 30 = 70, 30 − 30 = 0 and 25 − 25 = 0, so its largest regret is 70.

questions.onCorrect: Q's caution costs it 70 in the first state, where R pays 100.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Q's payoff in the first state. Regret is the gap between it and the best payoff, 100.
That is the best payoff in the first state. Regret is its gap from Q's payoff.
That is the gap between Q's own payoffs in the second and third states. Regret compares Q with the best payoff in each state.

questions.prompt: For options P, Q and R above, the best payoffs by state are 100, 30 and 25. Which option does minimax regret choose?
hints: Work out each option's regret in every state: the best payoff in that state minus the option's payoff.
Take the largest regret of each option, then choose the smallest of those three.
questions.onCorrect: P's regrets are 40, 10 and 25, so its largest, 40, is the smallest of the three largest regrets (Q's is 70 and R's is 55).

misconceptions.feedback: Q has the best worst payoff, which is maximin's test. Minimax regret compares the largest regret of each option.
R has the highest payoff in the first state, which is maximax's test. Minimax regret compares the largest regret of each option.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is tossed until it first lands heads. What is the probability that the first head comes on the third toss?
hints: The first two tosses must both be tails.
Multiply the chances of the three tosses.
Each toss has probability 1/2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first head on toss 3 needs tails, tails, heads: (1/2) × (1/2) × (1/2) = 1/8 = 0.125.

questions.onCorrect: A head first on toss n has probability (1/2)^n, which halves with each toss while the prize doubles.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance of a first head on the second toss.
That is the chance of heads on any one toss, and the first two tosses must be tails.

questions.prompt: A St Petersburg game pays 2^n dollars if the first head comes on toss n, but stops after 12 tosses and pays nothing if no head has come. What is its expected prize, in dollars?
hints: Each outcome contributes the same amount.
The terms for n = 1 to 12 each come to 1.
Count the terms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 12 possible outcomes contributes (1/2)^n × 2^n = 1, so the expected prize is 12.

questions.onCorrect: A cap turns an unbounded expectation into a modest one, which is closer to what players are willing to pay.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the largest prize, 2^12. It is reached with probability 1/4096.
That adds the prizes without weighting them by their chances.

questions.prompt: The gamble pays 16 or 64 with equal chances, and u(x) = √x. What is the utility of the 64 prize multiplied by its probability?
hints: Find u(64) first.
The square root of 64 is 8.
Take half of that.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: u(64) = 8, and half of 8 is 4.

questions.onCorrect: Together with 0.5 × u(16) = 2 this gives an expected utility of 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That is half of 64. Convert 64 to utility first.
That is u(64) itself. Weight it by the probability 0.5.

questions.prompt: With u(x) = √x, a gamble pays 0 or 100 with equal chances. What is its expected utility?
hints: Convert each prize to utility first.
√0 is 0 and √100 is 10.
Weight each by 0.5 and add.
questions.onCorrect: The gamble's expected utility of 5 is that of a sure 25, since √25 = 5, though its expected prize is 50.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the expected prize. Expected utility averages the utilities of the prizes.
That is the utility of the 100 alone. The 0 prize is equally likely.

questions.prompt: With u(x) = log₂ x, which sure amount, in dollars, has utility 3?
hints: Utility 3 means log₂ x = 3.
Undo the logarithm with a power of 2.
2 raised to the power 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: log₂ 8 = 3 because 2^3 = 8.

questions.onCorrect: A utility of 2 would correspond to a sure 4, which is where the St Petersburg game is valued under this curve.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the utility. The question asks for the amount that has it.
That is 3 squared. The inverse of log₂ is a power of 2.

questions.prompt: A friend says that anyone whose utility curve flattens, like √x, is irrational, because they sometimes turn down a gamble with a higher expected prize. Which reply is accurate?
hints: What does the utility curve describe?
Expected utility averages the worth of outcomes, not their amounts.

acceptedIdeas: The curve says what each amount is worth to that person, so it is not a mistake.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The curve says what each amount is worth to that person, so it is not a mistake.

questions.onCorrect: A concave curve records that extra money adds less worth, and choosing by expected utility is consistent with it.

choices.label: The expected prize is the only sound measure, so a flattening curve is a mistake.
Utility measures happiness, which cannot be averaged, so the curve is a mistake.
The curve changes the probabilities of the prizes, so it is not a mistake.
The curve says what each amount is worth to that person, so it is not a mistake.

misconceptions.feedback: The St Petersburg game shows that expected prize can recommend absurd prices, so it is not the only sound measure.
In decision theory utility is a number that represents preferences over gambles, not a measure of happiness.
The probabilities stay as they are, whatever the person's curve. Ask what the curve is applied to.

questions.prompt: With u(x) = √x, a gamble pays 4 or 36 with equal chances. What is its expected utility?
hints: Convert each prize to utility first.
Take the square root of each prize.
Weight each by 0.5 and add.
questions.onCorrect: A sure 16 has the same utility, √16 = 4, so the gamble is worth 16 to this chooser although its expected prize is 20.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the expected prize. Expected utility averages the utilities of the prizes.
That is the utility of the larger prize alone.

questions.prompt: A St Petersburg game pays 2^n dollars if the first head comes on toss n, but stops after 25 tosses and pays nothing if no head has come. What is its expected prize, in dollars?
hints: Each outcome contributes (1/2)^n × 2^n.
That product is 1 for every n.
Count the outcomes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 25 possible outcomes contributes 1 to the expectation, so the total is 25.

questions.onCorrect: Each extra toss allowed adds exactly 1 to the expected prize, so the expectation grows without limit as the cap is removed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the contribution of one outcome. The cap allows 25 of them.
Each outcome contributes 1, not 2.

questions.prompt: With u(x) = √x, a gamble pays 0 or 64 with equal chances. Which is preferred, the gamble or a sure 20?
hints: Find the gamble's expected utility.
Compare 4 with √20.
questions.onCorrect: The sure 20 has utility √20 ≈ 4.47, above the gamble's 4, though the gamble's expected prize of 32 is higher.

misconceptions.feedback: The gamble's expected prize is higher, but this chooser ranks gambles by expected utility. Compare that with the utility of a sure 20.
Work out the utility of a sure 20 and compare it with the gamble's expected utility.

questions.prompt: With u(x) = √x, which sure amount, in dollars, has a utility of 6?
hints: Utility 6 means √x = 6.
Undo the square root by squaring.
6 squared.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: √36 = 6, so the amount is 6² = 36.

questions.onCorrect: Squaring undoes the square root, which is how a utility is turned back into an amount.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the utility. The question asks for the amount that has it.
Squaring 6 gives the amount. Doubling it does not undo a square root.

questions.prompt: With u(x) = √x, a gamble pays 4 or 36 with equal chances, so its expected utility is 4. What sure amount has that utility?
hints: Set √x equal to the expected utility.
Square both sides.
The amount is the square of the utility.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: √x = 4 gives x = 4² = 16.

questions.onCorrect: A sure 16 is exactly as good as the gamble, though the gamble's expected prize is 20.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the expected utility. The certainty equivalent is the amount with that utility.
That is the expected prize. The certainty equivalent comes from the expected utility.

questions.prompt: With u(x) = √x, a gamble pays 4 or 100 with equal chances. Its certainty equivalent is 36 and its expected value is 52. What is the risk premium?
hints: The premium compares the expected value with the certainty equivalent.
Take the certainty equivalent from the expected value.
52 minus 36.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The risk premium is the expected value minus the certainty equivalent: 52 − 36 = 16.

questions.onCorrect: The chooser would give up as much as 16 of the gamble's expected prize to have a sure amount instead.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the certainty equivalent. The premium is its gap from the expected value.
That is the expected value. Subtract the certainty equivalent from it.

questions.prompt: With u(x) = x², a gamble pays 0 or 20 with equal chances. What is its certainty equivalent, to two decimal places?
hints: Square each prize to get its utility, and average.
The expected utility is 200.
Undo the squaring with a square root.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The expected utility is 0.5 × 0 + 0.5 × 400 = 200, and the amount with u(x) = x² = 200 is √200 ≈ 14.14.

questions.onCorrect: The certainty equivalent, 14.14, is above the expected value of 10, which is the sign of a risk-seeking curve.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the expected utility. Undo the squaring to get the amount.
That is the expected value. The certainty equivalent comes from the expected utility.

questions.prompt: A homeowner has wealth 100 and u(w) = √w. There is a 50% chance of a loss of 36, so wealth is 100 or 64. The expected utility is 9, which is the utility of a sure wealth of 81. What is the most the owner would pay for full insurance?
hints: Full insurance gives wealth 100 minus the premium.
The owner is indifferent when that wealth equals 81.
Subtract 81 from 100.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Insurance leaves the owner with 100 minus the premium. Paying up to 100 − 81 = 19 leaves wealth 81, which is as good as the risk.

questions.onCorrect: The expected loss is 18, so the owner would pay more, and an insurer charging between 18 and 19 would leave both better off.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the expected loss. A risk-averse owner would pay more than that.
That is the sure wealth with the same utility. The premium is how much wealth is given up from 100.

questions.prompt: A chooser with wealth 100 and u(w) = √w is offered a fair-coin bet: win 20 or lose 10. Staying at 100 has utility 10. What is the expected utility of taking the bet, to two decimal places?
hints: The bet leaves wealth at 120 or 90.
Take the square root of each wealth.
Average the two with weights 0.5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Wealth becomes 120 or 90, so the expected utility is 0.5 × √120 + 0.5 × √90 ≈ 0.5 × 10.954 + 0.5 × 9.487 ≈ 10.22.

questions.onCorrect: 10.22 exceeds 10, so a risk-averse chooser takes the bet, because the price of the risk is small beside the expected gain of 5.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the utility of staying at 100. The question asks about taking the bet.
That is expected wealth. Expected utility averages the utilities of the wealth levels.

questions.prompt: A chooser's utility curve bends upward, getting steeper as the amount rises. What is the chooser's attitude to risk?
hints: An upward-bending curve is convex.
The certainty equivalent of a gamble lies above its expected value.
questions.onCorrect: A convex curve puts the certainty equivalent above the expected value, so the chooser values the gamble above its average prize.

misconceptions.feedback: A risk-averse chooser has a concave curve, which flattens as the amount grows.
A risk-neutral chooser has a straight-line curve, with no bend.

questions.prompt: With u(x) = √x, a gamble pays 16 or 100 with equal chances. What is its certainty equivalent?
hints: First average the utilities of the two prizes.
The expected utility is 7.
Square it to get the amount.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The expected utility is 0.5 × 4 + 0.5 × 10 = 7, and the amount with utility 7 is 7² = 49.

questions.onCorrect: A sure 49 is as good as the gamble, although the gamble's expected prize is 58.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the expected utility. The certainty equivalent is the amount with that utility.
That is the expected value of the prizes. The certainty equivalent comes from expected utility.

questions.prompt: For the same gamble, 16 or 100 with equal chances and u(x) = √x, what is the risk premium?
hints: Find the expected value of the prizes.
It is 58, and the certainty equivalent is 49.
Subtract.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The expected value is 0.5 × 16 + 0.5 × 100 = 58 and the certainty equivalent is 49, so the premium is 58 − 49 = 9.

questions.onCorrect: The premium is positive for every risk-averse chooser, and it grows as the gamble becomes more spread out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the certainty equivalent. The premium is its gap from the expected value.
That is the expected value. Subtract the certainty equivalent.

questions.prompt: A chooser has u(x) = 3x. A fair-coin gamble pays 0 or 10, and the chooser's certainty equivalent is exactly 5. Which attitude is this?
hints: Compare the certainty equivalent with the expected value.
The expected value of the gamble is 5.
questions.onCorrect: A straight-line utility gives a certainty equivalent equal to the expected value, so the risk premium is 0.

misconceptions.feedback: A risk-averse chooser's certainty equivalent falls below the expected value, 5.
A risk-seeking chooser's certainty equivalent rises above the expected value, 5.

questions.prompt: Out of 10,000 people, 1% have a condition, and a test is positive for 90% of the people who have it. How many people have the condition and test positive?
hints: First count the people who have the condition.
That is 1% of 10,000.
Then take the share of that group that the test finds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1% of 10,000 is 100 people with the condition, and 90% of them test positive: 90.

questions.onCorrect: Counting people shows the pieces of a probability problem separately before they are combined.

misconceptions.feedback: That applies the test's detection rate to everyone tested. Only the 100 people who have the condition can be true positives.
That is everyone with the condition, whether or not the test finds them.

questions.prompt: Another condition has prevalence 5%, and the test has sensitivity 80% and a false-positive rate of 10%. Out of 1,000 people tested, how many test positive in total?
hints: Split the 1,000 into those who have it and those who do not.
40 true positives come from the 50 who have it.
Add the false positives from the other 950.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 50 people have it and 40 of them test positive; 950 do not, and 95 of them test positive. In total 40 + 95 = 135.

questions.onCorrect: Of the 135 positives, 95 are healthy people, which is why a positive result is weaker evidence than the 80% sensitivity suggests.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only true positives. People without the condition also test positive.
That counts only false positives. The people with the condition who test positive are included too.

questions.prompt: Of 135 positive results, 40 come from people with the condition. What percentage of positives are true, to one decimal place?
hints: Divide the true positives by all positives.
The positives total 135.
40 divided by 135, as a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: The posterior of 29.6% is far above the 5% prior and far below the 80% sensitivity.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sensitivity, the chance of a positive given the condition. The question asks for the reverse.
That is the prior. The positive result raised it.

questions.prompt: 20% of mail is spam. The word 'prize' appears in 60% of spam and in 3% of other mail. What is the probability that a message containing 'prize' is spam, to two decimal places?
hints: Find the share of all mail that is spam and has the word.
Find the share that is other mail and has the word.
Divide the first by the sum of the two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Spam with the word: 0.2 × 0.6 = 0.12. Other mail with the word: 0.8 × 0.03 = 0.024. So the chance is 0.12 ÷ (0.12 + 0.024) = 5/6 ≈ 0.83.

questions.onCorrect: The word is 20 times more common in spam than elsewhere, which outweighs the 4-to-1 prior against spam.

misconceptions.feedback: That is P('prize' | spam), the transposed conditional.
That is the share of all mail that is spam containing the word. The posterior divides it by all mail containing the word.

questions.prompt: A test has a likelihood ratio of 10 for a positive result. Before the test the odds of disease are 1 to 4, a probability of 0.2. What is the probability after one positive result, to two decimal places?
hints: Multiply the odds in favour by the likelihood ratio.
1 to 4 becomes 10 to 4.
Probability is the first number over the total.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The odds become 1 × 10 : 4 = 10 : 4, so the probability is 10 ÷ 14 ≈ 0.71.

questions.onCorrect: Multiplying odds by the likelihood ratio is the shortcut that makes repeated updating easy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the odds 10 to 4 written as one number. A probability is a share of the whole, not the ratio of the two parts.
That is the prior. The positive result should raise it.

questions.prompt: A test has a likelihood ratio of 10, and two independent positive results arrive. Which update of the odds is right?
hints: Each independent result carries its own evidence.
Independent evidence multiplies odds.

acceptedIdeas: Multiply by 10 twice, a factor of 100
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Multiply by 10 twice, a factor of 100

questions.onCorrect: Independent results each multiply the odds by their likelihood ratio, so two give a factor of 100 on the odds.

choices.label: Multiply by 10 twice, a factor of 100
Add the ratios, giving a factor of 20
Average the ratios, giving a factor of 10
Multiply by 10 once, since the second result repeats the first

misconceptions.feedback: Likelihood ratios multiply the odds. They are not added.
A second independent result is new evidence, so it multiplies the odds again.
Averaging would discard the second result. Each one multiplies the odds.

questions.prompt: A condition has prevalence 2%. A test is positive for 80% of people with it and for 10% of people without it. Out of 10,000 people tested, how many test positive in total?
hints: Count the people with the condition, then those without.
The true positives are 160.
Add the false positives from the 9,800.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 200 people have it and 160 of them test positive; 9,800 do not and 980 of them test positive; 160 + 980 = 1,140.

questions.onCorrect: Of the 1,140 positives, 980 are false, so most positive results here come from people without the condition.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only true positives. Healthy people also test positive.
That counts only false positives. People with the condition who test positive are included too.

questions.prompt: For the same test and prevalence, what is the probability of the condition after one positive result, as a percentage to one decimal place?
hints: Divide the true positives by all positives.
The true positives are 160 and the positives total 1,140.
160 ÷ 1,140 as a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 160 of the 1,140 positives have the condition: 160 ÷ 1,140 ≈ 0.140, or 14.0%.

questions.onCorrect: The result is 14.0%, far below the 80% sensitivity, because the condition is rare.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sensitivity, P(positive | condition). The question asks for P(condition | positive).
That is the prior. The positive result raised it.

questions.prompt: 30% of mail is spam. The word 'free' appears in 50% of spam and in 5% of other mail. What is the probability that a message containing 'free' is spam, to two decimal places?
hints: Find the share of all mail that is spam with the word.
Find the share that is other mail with the word.
Divide the first by their sum.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Spam with the word: 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15. Other mail with the word: 0.7 × 0.05 = 0.035. So the chance is 0.15 ÷ 0.185 ≈ 0.81.

questions.onCorrect: The word is ten times as common in spam as in other mail, and spam is common enough to make the posterior high.

misconceptions.feedback: That is P('free' | spam). The question asks for P(spam | 'free').
That is the share of all mail that is spam with the word. Divide it by all mail with the word.

questions.prompt: The project loses 30 if it fails and pays 100 if it succeeds, and not investing pays 0. Suppose you learn before deciding that it will fail. What payoff do you get from your best choice?
hints: Compare investing with not investing when failure is certain.
Investing loses money in that case.
Not investing pays nothing.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Knowing the project fails, you do not invest, and the payoff is 0.

questions.onCorrect: With the failure known in advance, the loss is avoided, which is where the value of information comes from.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the payoff of investing in a failure. With the failure known, you would not invest.
That is the payoff in the success state, not the failure state.

questions.prompt: A second project succeeds with probability 0.5 and pays 60, or fails with probability 0.5 and loses 20. Not investing pays 0. What is the expected value of the best choice now?
hints: Find the expected value of investing.
Weight each payoff by its probability of one half.
Compare the result with 0.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Investing is worth 0.5 × 60 − 0.5 × 20 = 20, which beats 0, so the best choice now is worth 20.

questions.onCorrect: The best choice now is the larger of the two expected values, here 20 for investing.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the loss in the failure state.
Investing has a positive expected value here, so it beats not investing.

questions.prompt: For the second project, the best choice now is worth 20, and learning the state first is worth 0.5 × 60 + 0.5 × 0 = 30. What is the expected value of perfect information?
hints: Subtract the value now from the value with the forecast.
The value with the forecast is 30.
30 minus 20.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The expected value of perfect information is 30 − 20 = 10.

questions.onCorrect: That 10 is also the expected regret of investing, 0.5 × 20, the loss it risks on average.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value with the forecast. The EVPI is its gap above the value now.
That is the value now. Subtract it from 30.

questions.prompt: For the first project, the perfect forecast is worth 40 before its price. The best choice now is worth 22. What is the expected value of buying a forecast that costs 14?
hints: Take the price off the value with the forecast.
The value with the forecast is 40.
40 minus 14.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The forecast gives 40, and its price takes off 14, so buying is worth 40 − 14 = 26, which beats 22.

questions.onCorrect: Because 26 beats 22, the forecast pays for itself, and the margin is 4, the EVPI of 18 less the price of 14.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the EVPI, the most you would pay. The question asks for the value after paying 14.
The price is a cost, so it comes off.

questions.prompt: A project pays 100 with probability 0.4 and 0 with probability 0.6. It costs nothing to enter, and not investing pays 0. What is the expected value of perfect information?
hints: Would a forecast ever make you choose differently?
Investing here never loses money.
If the choice never changes, the information adds nothing.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Investing is never worse than not investing, so the best choice is the same in both states, and a forecast cannot improve it: the EVPI is 0.

questions.onCorrect: Information is worth only the decisions it changes, so a forecast that would never change the choice is worth nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the expected value of investing, and it is the same with or without the forecast.
That is the probability that the project pays nothing. Ask what a forecast would change about the decision.

questions.prompt: The first project's chance of success rises to 0.8, with the same payoffs: 100 on success, −30 on failure, and 0 for not investing. What is the expected value of perfect information now?
hints: Recompute the best choice now with the new probability.
Then the value with perfect information.
The EVPI is also the expected regret of investing, 0.2 × 30.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The best choice now is 0.8 × 100 − 0.2 × 30 = 74. With perfect information it is 0.8 × 100 + 0.2 × 0 = 80. So the EVPI is 80 − 74 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: As the chance of success rises, the forecast has less to correct, so its ceiling falls from 18 to 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the EVPI at the old probability, 0.4. The probability has changed.
That is the value of the best choice now. The EVPI is the gain over it.

questions.prompt: A forecaster who is right 90% of the time offers a forecast of the first project for 15. The EVPI is 18. What follows?
hints: Is EVPI the value of this forecast, or a limit on it?
The forecast is not perfect.

acceptedIdeas: The price alone does not settle it, as this forecast is worth under 18.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The price alone does not settle it, as this forecast is worth under 18.

questions.onCorrect: The EVPI bounds the value of any forecast from above, so a price below it does not prove a forecast is worth buying.

choices.label: Buy it, because the price of 15 is below the EVPI of 18.
Buy it, because 90% of 18 is 16.2, which is more than the price of 15.
Decline it, because a forecast that is sometimes wrong has no value.
The price alone does not settle it, as this forecast is worth under 18.

misconceptions.feedback: The EVPI is the value of a perfect forecast. Ask whether this forecast is perfect.
Accuracy does not scale the EVPI like that. The worth of an imperfect forecast depends on how it changes the decision, which the next lesson computes.
An imperfect forecast can still change decisions, and any decision it changes is worth something.

questions.prompt: A project succeeds with probability 0.25 and pays 200, or fails with probability 0.75 and loses 20. Not investing pays 0. What is the expected value of the best choice now?
hints: Find the expected value of investing.
Compare with 0.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Investing is worth 0.25 × 200 − 0.75 × 20 = 50 − 15 = 35, which beats not investing at 0.

questions.onCorrect: Investing is the best choice now, worth 35.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the loss in the failure state.
Investing has a positive expected value, so it beats not investing.

questions.prompt: For the same project, what is the expected value of perfect information?
hints: Find the value when the state is known before choosing.
You invest only on success, so the value is 0.25 × 200.
Subtract the value of the best choice now, 35.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With perfect information you invest only on success: 0.25 × 200 + 0.75 × 0 = 50. The EVPI is 50 − 35 = 15.

questions.onCorrect: The same 15 is the expected regret of investing, 0.75 × 20.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value with perfect information. Subtract the value now.
That is the value now. The EVPI is the gain above it.

questions.prompt: A consultant offers a guaranteed forecast of that project for 20. The expected value of perfect information is 15. What should you do?
hints: Compare the price with the most any information can be worth.
The EVPI is that most.
questions.onCorrect: A perfect forecast adds 15 on average, so paying 20 for it loses 5.

misconceptions.feedback: Perfect or not, a forecast is worth buying only if its price is less than what it adds. Compare 20 with what it adds.
The value with the forecast is 50, but the price should be compared with what the forecast adds over choosing now.
The EVPI is given in the question, so the comparison can be made.

questions.prompt: A project succeeds with probability 0.4. A test says good with probability 0.8 if the project will succeed and with probability 0.3 if it will fail. What is the probability that the test says good?
hints: A good result can come from either a success or a failure.
Add the two routes: success then good, failure then good.
Weight each likelihood by its prior.
questions.onCorrect: Before the test you know only the chance of each result, which is where the test node's branch probabilities come from.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance of good given success. Failures also produce good results.
That is the plain average of 0.8 and 0.3, ignoring that success and failure are not equally likely.

questions.prompt: A project succeeds with probability 0.4. A test says bad with probability 0.2 if the project will succeed, and a bad result has probability 0.5 overall. After a bad result, what is the probability that the project succeeds?
hints: Find the chance of success together with a bad result.
That is the prior times the chance of bad given success.
Divide by the chance of a bad result.
questions.onCorrect: A bad result cuts the chance of success from 0.4 to 0.16, which is what turns the choice to not investing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance of a bad result given success. The question asks for the chance of success given a bad result.
That is the joint probability. Divide it by the chance of a bad result.

questions.prompt: After a good result the chance of success is 0.64, so the chance of failure is 0.36. What is the expected value of investing, paying 100 on success and losing 30 on failure?
hints: Weight the payoffs by the posterior probabilities, not the prior ones.
The success term is 64.
Subtract the weighted loss.
questions.onCorrect: With the posterior as the chance of success, investing is worth 53.2, well above the 22 it was worth before the test.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the prior probabilities. After a good result use the posterior.
That leaves out the weighted loss of 10.8.

questions.prompt: The test leads to an expected value of 26.6 before its cost. What is the expected value of buying it when it costs 4?
hints: Take the cost off the total value with the test.
The value with the test is 26.6.
26.6 minus 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The cost comes off the value with the test: 26.6 − 4 = 22.6.

questions.onCorrect: Since 22.6 still exceeds the 22 from choosing now, the test is worth buying at that price, though only just.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the EVSI. The question asks for the value of the test after the cost.
A cost is subtracted, not added.

questions.prompt: A weaker test says good with probability 0.6 if the project will succeed and 0.5 if it will fail. It still leaves investing worth more than not investing after either result. What is the expected value of sample information for this weak test?
hints: Does either result change which option is best?
Investing is still best after both results.
A test that never changes the choice adds no value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The best choice after either result is the same as the best choice now, to invest, so the test never changes the decision and adds nothing: the EVSI is 0.

questions.onCorrect: Information is worth only the decisions it changes, so a test that cannot move the choice is worth nothing at any price.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the EVSI of the stronger test. The weak test never changes the decision.
That is the EVPI. A real test's value cannot exceed it, and a weak one is far below.

questions.prompt: The test has an EVSI of 4.6 and costs 5. Should you buy it?
hints: Compare the cost with the test's own value, not with the EVPI.
The value gained from the test is 4.6.
questions.onCorrect: The test adds 4.6 on average and costs 5, so buying it loses 0.4. The EVPI is a ceiling only for a perfect forecast.

choices.label: Yes, because it is better than no test

misconceptions.feedback: Being better than no test is not enough on its own. Compare the price with the test's value.
The EVPI is the value of a perfect forecast. This test is worth only its own EVSI.
Both the EVSI and the cost are given, so the comparison can be made.

questions.prompt: Suppose the prior chance of success were only 0.2, with the same test: good with probability 0.8 given success and 0.3 given failure. After a good result, what is the probability of success?
hints: Find the chance of a good result with the new prior.
Divide the success-and-good share by P(good).
questions.onCorrect: With a lower prior the same good result gives a lower posterior: the test's 80% accuracy is not the probability of success.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance of good given success. The posterior also depends on the prior.
That is the posterior for a prior of 0.4. The prior here is 0.2.

questions.prompt: A project succeeds with probability 0.3 and pays 100, or fails with probability 0.7 and loses 20. A test says good with probability 0.9 if it will succeed and 0.2 if it will fail. What is the probability that the test says good?
hints: A good result can come from a success or a failure.
Add success-then-good and failure-then-good.
0.27 plus another term.
questions.onCorrect: The test node's branch probability is 0.41, and the posterior after a good result is 0.27 ÷ 0.41.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance of good given success. Failures also produce good results.
That is the plain average of 0.9 and 0.2, ignoring the prior.

questions.prompt: For the same project and test, not investing pays 0. The best choice now is investing, worth 0.3 × 100 − 0.7 × 20 = 16. After a bad result investing is not worth it, and after a good result it is. What is the expected value of sample information?
hints: You invest only after a good result.
The value with the test is the success-and-good share times 100, less the failure-and-good share times 20.
Subtract the value of the best choice now, 16.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The value with the test is 0.3 × 0.9 × 100 − 0.7 × 0.2 × 20 = 27 − 2.8 = 24.2, because you invest only after a good result. The EVSI is 24.2 − 16 = 8.2.

questions.onCorrect: The test is worth 8.2 on average, which is less than the EVPI of 0.7 × 20 = 14.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value with the test. The EVSI is its gain over the best choice now.
That is the EVPI. The real test is worth less.

questions.prompt: The test costs 6, and its EVSI is 8.2. What should you do?
hints: Compare the cost with the EVSI.
The EVSI is the average gain from the test.

acceptedIdeas: Buy it: its EVSI exceeds the cost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Buy it: its EVSI exceeds the cost

questions.onCorrect: The test adds 8.2 on average and costs 6, a net gain of 2.2 over choosing now.

choices.label: Buy it: its EVSI exceeds the cost
Buy it only if it is perfect
Decline it: the cost exceeds its EVSI

misconceptions.feedback: Compare the cost with the EVSI and see which is larger.
A real test can be worth buying without being perfect.
The EVSI is known, so the comparison can be made.

questions.prompt: A person prefers A to B and B to C, but prefers C to A. Which axiom of expected-utility theory does this break?
hints: It concerns a chain of preferences.
If A is preferred to B and B to C, then A should beat C.
questions.onCorrect: Transitivity requires that preferring A to B and B to C means preferring A to C, and a cycle of preferences breaks it.

misconceptions.feedback: Independence concerns mixing a gamble with a third one. This is a chain of three simple preferences.
Continuity concerns small changes in probability. This is a chain of three preferences.

questions.prompt: A person with cyclic preferences pays 2 for each swap and goes twice round the cycle of three swaps. How much do they pay in total?
hints: Count the swaps in one full cycle.
Two cycles make 6 swaps.
Multiply by the fee of 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two cycles of three swaps make 6 swaps, and 6 × 2 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: Each swap looks like a gain to the person, so the loss accumulates without any step feeling like a mistake.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of swaps. Each one costs 2.
That is the fee for one swap. They pay it on every swap.

questions.prompt: Gamble D pays 5 million with probability 0.10 and nothing otherwise. What is its expected value, in millions?
hints: Weight the prize by its probability.
The only prize is 5 million.
0.10 times 5.
questions.onCorrect: That is far below the 1.39 million of gamble B, yet many people take D and also A, which is the puzzle.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the prize. Its probability is only 0.10.
That is the probability. Multiply it by the prize.

questions.prompt: Set u(nothing) = 0 and u(1M) = 1. Preferring A to B then requires 0.11 > 0.10 × u(5M). Below what value of u(5M) does that hold?
hints: Divide both sides by 0.10.
The right side becomes u(5M).
0.11 divided by 0.10.
questions.onCorrect: Preferring D to C requires the opposite, u(5M) > 1.1, so no number can satisfy both.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the left side. Divide it by 0.10 to isolate u(5M).
Check the decimal places in the division.

questions.prompt: The common pattern of choosing A over B and D over C cannot come from any utility function. Which axiom does it break?
hints: The two pairs differ only in what happens in the shared 89%.
Which axiom says a common part should not change the preference?
questions.onCorrect: Independence says that mixing both gambles with the same third gamble should not reverse a preference, and here the shared 89% does reverse it.

misconceptions.feedback: The pattern involves two separate pairs, not a chain of three preferences.
Continuity concerns small changes in probability, and it is not the axiom the shared 89% breaks.

questions.prompt: A friend says that choosing A over B and D over C just shows that the chooser's utility for money curves, with each extra million worth less. What is the accurate reply?
hints: The inequality for the first choice is the reverse of the one for the second.
It holds for any values of u(0), u(1M) and u(5M).

acceptedIdeas: No: the two choices contradict each other for every utility function, curved or not
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No: the two choices contradict each other for every utility function, curved or not

questions.onCorrect: Curvature changes u(5M) relative to u(1M), but the two inequalities contradict each other whatever its value.

choices.label: Right: a sufficiently curved utility function explains both choices
No: the choices show the chooser is wrong to maximise utility at all
No: the two choices contradict each other for every utility function, curved or not
Right: a straight-line utility function explains both choices

misconceptions.feedback: Whatever value curvature gives u(5M), the two preferences require u(5M) to be both below and above the same number.
Linear utility is one special case, and the inequalities still contradict each other.
The result is narrower: no utility function fits that pair of choices, which shows where the theory's axioms bind.

questions.prompt: A person prefers gamble X to gamble Y, but prefers a half-and-half mixture of Y with Z to the same mixture of X with Z. Which axiom does this break?
hints: The mixtures use the same third gamble, Z.
Which axiom says a common part should not reverse a preference?
questions.onCorrect: Independence requires that adding the same third gamble to both options leaves the preference unchanged.

misconceptions.feedback: Transitivity concerns chains of preferences. This pattern involves mixing.
Continuity concerns small changes in probability, not a shared mixture.

questions.prompt: A person prefers A to B, B to C and C to A, and pays 5 for each swap to a preferred item. Starting with C, how much do they pay after going once round the cycle?
hints: Count the swaps in one trip round the cycle.
There are three swaps.
Multiply by the fee of 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One trip round the cycle takes three swaps, so they pay 3 × 5 = 15 and are back where they began.

questions.onCorrect: After the three swaps they hold the item they started with, and are poorer by the fees.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fee for one swap. A trip round the cycle takes three.
A trip round the cycle takes three swaps, not two.

questions.prompt: Gamble B has been replaced by a new gamble that pays 2 million with probability 0.89, 10 million with probability 0.10 and nothing with probability 0.01. What is its expected value, in millions?
hints: Multiply each prize by its probability.
The products are 1.78 and 1.0, and 0.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: Expected value is a useful comparison, but the Allais pattern shows that choices can depart from it in a way no utility function repairs.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the prizes without weighting them by probability.
That is the expected value of the original gamble B. The prizes here are larger.

questions.prompt: Programme B saves all 600 people with probability one third and nobody with probability two thirds. What is the expected number of people saved?
hints: Weight each outcome by its probability.
One third of 600.
questions.onCorrect: Programme A saves 200 for sure, so both have the same expected result, and a preference between them depends on the description.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number saved if the gamble succeeds. It succeeds with probability one third.
That is the expected number of deaths under programme D. The question is about the number saved.

questions.prompt: Programme D means nobody dies with probability one third and 600 people die with probability two thirds. What is the expected number of deaths?
hints: Weight the deaths by their probabilities.
Two thirds of 600.
questions.onCorrect: That equals the 400 deaths of programme C, so C and D differ only in wording from A and B.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the expected number saved. The question asks for deaths.
That is the deaths if the gamble fails. It fails with probability two thirds.

questions.prompt: A 50/50 gamble wins 100 or loses 60, and losses count twice as much as gains. The gamble's value is its gain term plus its loss term, and the gain term is 0.5 × 100 = 50. What is the loss term?
hints: Double the loss first.
Doubling 60 gives 120, and it stays a loss.
Weight by 0.5.
questions.onCorrect: With the gain term of 50, the value is 50 − 60 = −10, though the expected money value is +20.

misconceptions.feedback: A loss keeps its minus sign.
That does not double the loss before weighting it.

questions.prompt: With losses counting twice, a 50/50 gamble risks a loss of 70. What win would make the gamble's value exactly zero?
hints: Set 0.5 × w equal to the weighted loss.
The loss counts double before it is weighted by 0.5.
Solve for w.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The value is 0.5 × w − 0.5 × 140, which is zero when w = 140.

questions.onCorrect: The win must exceed twice the loss before a loss-averse chooser accepts an even-chance bet, though the expected money gain turns positive at 70.

misconceptions.feedback: That makes the expected money value zero, but the doubled loss still outweighs the gain.

questions.prompt: You paid 80 for a ticket to an event, and the money is not refundable. Going costs 30 in travel and is worth 20 to you. By how much does going beat skipping? Use a negative number if skipping is better.
hints: Leave out the 80, which you lose whatever you do.
Going gains 20 and costs 30.
Compare the net with the 0 for skipping.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Going gains 20 and costs 30, a net of −10, while skipping gives 0. The 80 is gone in either case.

questions.onCorrect: The price of the ticket appears in both options, so it cannot separate them.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the 80, which is gone whether or not you go.
Going costs 30 and is worth 20, so it falls short.

questions.prompt: Two wordings describe the same programmes with the same probabilities, one in lives saved and one in deaths, and people choose differently in the two. What does that show?
hints: Compare the outcomes and probabilities in the two wordings.
The expected numbers are identical.

acceptedIdeas: Choices can shift with the wording even though the outcomes are identical
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Choices can shift with the wording even though the outcomes are identical

questions.onCorrect: The outcomes and probabilities are identical, so a shift in choice comes from the frame and not from the numbers.

choices.label: The lives-saved wording has a higher expected number saved
The wordings describe different outcomes, so different choices are consistent
Choices can shift with the wording even though the outcomes are identical
The deaths wording has a higher expected number of deaths

misconceptions.feedback: Check whether the outcomes differ: 200 saved out of 600 leaves how many dead, and is the gamble the same?
